chapters.title: Rescue pictured through storm and battle
chapters.summary: The speaker loves the LORD, his rock and fortress. The cords of death once wrapped around him, and he cried out. The earth shook, and God came down in smoke, fire, and storm. He reached from on high and drew the speaker out of deep waters. He brought him into a wide place. God lights his lamp and trains his hands for battle. With God’s help he overcomes his enemies. He praises the LORD, who shows kindness to David and his line.
chapters.meaning: Verses 7–15 describe an earthquake, thunder, hail, and the sea floor laid bare. All of it answers one man’s cry (verse 6). Verse 16 then narrows that power to a single act. A hand reaches down, takes hold, and pulls him from the water. The scale of the storm shows the worth of the one rescued. Verse 19 calls the result “a large place,” the opposite of the cords. Second Samuel 22 gives the same song.

lds.text: How do the storm images describe the force of rescue?

chapters.historicalNote: Large images give form to deliverance. The heading connects the song with David and Saul.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: Rescue is described through an overwhelming landscape
contextNote.text: Verses 7–15 describe an earthquake, thunder, hail, and the sea floor laid bare. All of it answers one man’s cry (verse 6). Verse 16 then narrows that power to a single act. A hand reaches down, takes hold, and pulls him from the water. The scale of the storm shows the worth of the one rescued. Verse 19 calls the result “a large place,” the opposite of the cords. Second Samuel 22 gives the same song.

chapters.title: The heavens and God’s teaching
chapters.summary: The heavens tell God’s glory without speech or words. Their message goes out through all the earth. The sun runs its course like a strong man, and nothing hides from its heat. The LORD’s law is perfect and restores the soul. His commands are right, pure, and sweeter than honey. The speaker asks who can see his own errors. He asks to be cleared of hidden faults. He prays that his words and thoughts will please the LORD.
chapters.meaning: The poem moves in three steps. Verses 1–6 look at the sky, and verses 7–11 at the LORD’s law. Verses 12–14 look at one person. The view narrows from the universe to a text to a heart. Nothing hides from the sun (verse 6), and the law also exposes. So verse 12 asks about faults he cannot see. Verse 14 offers his mouth and his thoughts for inspection.

lds.text: How does attention to creation lead toward examining words and thoughts?

chapters.historicalNote: The poem moves from the visible world to the conduct of one person.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: The poem narrows from skies to speech
contextNote.text: The poem moves in three steps. Verses 1–6 look at the sky, and verses 7–11 at the LORD’s law. Verses 12–14 look at one person. chapters.title: A prayer for the king before danger
chapters.summary: The people pray for their king before a battle. They ask the LORD to answer him in the day of trouble. They ask God to send help from the sanctuary and remember his offerings. They will shout for joy at his victory. A single voice says the LORD saves his anointed. Some trust in chariots and horses. The people trust in the name of the LORD. They ask the King to answer when they call.
chapters.meaning: In verses 1–5 the people speak to their king as “you.” In verse 6 one voice says, “Now I know.” Verse 7 then compares two kinds of trust. Chariots and horses were the strongest weapons of the time. Deuteronomy 17:16 told Israel’s king not to build up horses. The people name the LORD’s name as their weapon. Verse 9 asks “the King” to answer, so the human king also has a King.

lds.text: Why do the people trust God more than horses and chariots?

chapters.historicalNote: Chariots and horses represent strength, but the people place their trust in God.

contextNote.title: A community speaks before a battle
contextNote.text: In verses 1–5 the people speak to their king as “you.” In verse 6 one voice says, “Now I know.” Verse 7 then compares two kinds of trust. Chariots and horses were the strongest weapons of the time. Deuteronomy 17:16 told Israel’s king not to build up horses. The people name the LORD’s name as their weapon. Verse 9 asks “the King” to answer, so the human king also has a King.

chapters.title: Thanks for the king’s deliverance
chapters.summary: The king rejoices in the LORD’s strength. God has given him his heart’s desire. God set a crown of fine gold on his head. He asked for life, and God gave it. His glory is great because God saved him. The king trusts in the LORD and will not be shaken. God’s hand will find all his enemies. The people sing and praise God’s power.
chapters.meaning: Psalm 20 asked that the king receive his heart’s desire (20:4). Verse 2 here says God has given it. The two poems form a request and its answer. Verse 7 is the hinge of this one. The king is secure because he trusts and because the Most High is kind. Verse 3 says God set the crown on him. The poem begins and ends with “your strength,” meaning God’s (verses 1 and 13).

lds.text: How does the king respond to the help he receives?

chapters.title: Abandonment, suffering, and praise
chapters.summary: The speaker cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” He calls day and night and gets no answer. He recalls that his fathers trusted God and were rescued. People mock him and shake their heads. He is poured out like water, and his bones are out of joint. Men stare at him and cast lots for his clothing. He begs God not to be far away. Then he praises God, and the ends of the earth turn to the LORD.
chapters.meaning: The first line accuses and still says “my God” twice. The speaker complains to the one he feels has left. The poem then swings between pain and memory. Complaint and memory alternate through verses 1–10. From verse 22 it becomes praise. Verse 24 says God has not hidden his face. Jesus speaks the first line on the cross in Mark 15:34.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects this suffering with Jesus Christ’s crucifixion. Crucifixion means death on a cross. How does the prayer change toward its end?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer changes from isolation to shared praise. The painful opening remains part of its witness.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

chapters.title: The Lord as shepherd and host
chapters.summary: The speaker says the LORD is his shepherd, so he lacks nothing. The shepherd leads him to green pastures and still waters. He restores his soul and guides him in right paths. Even in the darkest valley the speaker fears no evil. God’s rod and staff comfort him. God prepares a table for him in front of his enemies. God anoints his head with oil, and his cup overflows. Goodness and kindness will follow him all his life.
chapters.meaning: The poem changes its picture at verse 5. The shepherd of verses 1–4 becomes a host with a table. A host’s duties are all there: food, oil for the head, a full cup. The enemies have not gone; the meal is served in front of them. The poem also changes its grammar. “He” becomes “you” in verse 4, in the dark valley. In verse 6 goodness “follows” him, where enemies usually pursue.

chapters.historicalNote: The shepherd’s care continues through the dark valley. The poem does not promise a path without danger.

chapters.title: Who may enter before the King of glory?
chapters.summary: The earth and everything in it belong to the LORD. He founded it on the seas. The poem asks who may go up the LORD’s hill and stand there. The answer is one with clean hands and a pure heart. That person does not trust in lies or swear falsely. Then the gates are told to lift up their heads. The King of glory is coming in. He is the LORD of Armies, strong and mighty in battle.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 says the owner of the whole earth has one hill as his own. Verse 3 asks who may enter there. Verse 4 names hands, heart, and speech. Hands are deeds, the heart is intent, and oaths are words. No offering is mentioned. The questions and answers read like an exchange at a gate (verses 3, 8, 10). Worshipers go up in verse 3, and the King comes in at verse 7.

chapters.title: Guidance, forgiveness, and loneliness
chapters.summary: The speaker lifts his soul to the LORD and asks not to be shamed. He asks God to show him his ways and teach him his paths. He asks God to remember mercy and not the sins of his youth. The LORD is good and teaches sinners the way. The speaker asks pardon for his guilt, which is great. He is lonely and afflicted. The troubles of his heart have grown. He asks God to guard his life and redeem Israel.
chapters.meaning: The word “remember” comes three times in verses 6–7. God should remember his own mercies, which are ancient. He should not remember the speaker’s early sins. He should remember the speaker himself, according to his kindness. The request is about which memory will govern. Its ground is God’s goodness, not any claim of improvement. Verse 11 even asks for pardon because the guilt is great.

lds.text: How does admitting failure make room for learning?

chapters.historicalNote: Learning requires humility. The request for guidance includes an honest account of past failures.

chapters.title: Integrity and love for worship
chapters.summary: The speaker asks the LORD to judge him, since he has walked in integrity. He invites God to test his heart and mind. He keeps God’s kindness before his eyes. He does not sit with deceitful people. He washes his hands in innocence and walks around the altar. He sings thanks and loves the house where God’s glory lives. He asks not to be swept away with men who take bribes. He asks to be redeemed and shown mercy.
chapters.meaning: Priests washed before they served at the altar (Exodus 30:17–21). Elders washed their hands to declare innocence in Deuteronomy 21:6. Verse 6 draws on that practice. The speaker’s claim to integrity has a goal. He wants to stand at the altar among those who give thanks (verses 7–8). It is not a claim to need nothing. Verse 11 still asks, “Redeem me, and be merciful to me.”

chapters.title: Seeking God’s face amid fear
chapters.summary: The LORD is the speaker’s light and salvation, so he fears no one. Even if an army camps against him, he will be confident. He has asked one thing: to live in the LORD’s house and see his beauty. God will hide him in his shelter in the day of trouble. Then the tone changes, and he begs God to hear him. He asks God not to hide his face or abandon him. False witnesses have risen against him. He tells himself to wait for the LORD and be strong.
chapters.meaning: The first half of the poem is confident (verses 1–6). The second half pleads (verses 7–14). Verse 4 stands in the confident half and is already a request. With armies around him, he asks for “one thing.” It is not victory or even safety. He wants to live near God, look, and ask. The last verse tells him to wait, so the request is not yet granted.

lds.text: What kind of courage does waiting require?

chapters.historicalNote: Confidence and pleading stand together. Waiting requires courage while danger remains.

chapters.title: Do not remain silent
chapters.summary: The speaker calls to the LORD, his rock, and asks him not to be deaf. If God is silent, he will be like those who go down to the pit. He lifts his hands toward the holy place. He asks not to be dragged off with the wicked. They speak peace to neighbors with harm in their hearts. Then he blesses the LORD for hearing his cry. The LORD is his strength and shield. He asks God to save his people and carry them forever.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 joins two pictures that do not fit: a rock that might be deaf. The speaker’s whole safety rests on being heard. He says God’s silence would be like death, the “pit.” Verse 2 asks God to hear the voice of his pleading. Verse 6 uses the same words to say that God has heard. Nothing else is reported between request and thanks. Verses 8–9 widen the prayer to all the people.

chapters.title: The Lord’s voice over the storm
chapters.summary: The poem calls the heavenly beings to give the LORD glory. The LORD’s voice sounds over the waters and thunders. His voice breaks the cedars of Lebanon. It makes the mountains skip like a calf. It strikes with flashes of fire and shakes the wilderness. It strips the forests bare. In his temple everyone says, “Glory!” The LORD sits as king forever and blesses his people with peace.
chapters.meaning: “The LORD’s voice” comes seven times in this poem. The voice is thunder, and the poem follows a storm. Verse 3 hears it over the sea. Verses 5–6 see it break trees in Lebanon to the north. Verse 8 follows it into the wilderness. All that power ends in two gifts in verse 11. The last word of the poem is “peace.”

lds.text: How does the ending change the mood of the storm?

chapters.historicalNote: The powerful storm ends with a blessing of peace for the people.

chapters.title: Mourning becomes dancing
chapters.summary: The speaker praises the LORD for lifting him up. He cried for help, and God healed him and kept him from the grave. God’s anger lasts a moment, and his favor a lifetime. Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning. In good times the speaker said he would never be shaken. Then God hid his face, and he was terrified. He pleaded for his life. God turned his mourning into dancing and clothed him with gladness.
chapters.meaning: Verse 6 is a confession about the speaker’s good years. He said, “I shall never be moved.” Verse 7 corrects him. His mountain stood firm only by God’s favor. He had taken a gift for his own strength. When God hid his face, the confidence was gone at once. The poem thanks God for a rescue and also for that lesson.

lds.text: What did the speaker learn when earlier confidence failed?

chapters.historicalNote: Prosperity once seemed secure. Loss taught the speaker to recognize dependence on God.

chapters.title: Entrusting life to God
chapters.summary: The speaker takes refuge in the LORD and asks for quick rescue. He commits his spirit into God’s hand. He is in distress, and grief wastes his eyes and body. Neighbors dread him, and he is forgotten like a dead man. He hears whispering and plots against his life. Yet he says, “You are my God,” and that his times are in God’s hand. He praises the goodness God stores up for those who fear him. He tells all who hope in the LORD to be strong.
chapters.meaning: Verse 13 describes a threat made of talk. He hears slander, and people plan together to take his life. Jeremiah 20:10 uses almost the same words, “terror on every side.” Verse 14 answers with “But I trust in you.” His trust is stated inside the danger, before it ends. Verse 15 places his “times” in God’s hand, against those who plot his end. Jesus speaks verse 5 from the cross in Luke 23:46.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects this prayer with Jesus Christ’s words. What help does the speaker still request?

chapters.historicalNote: Entrusting the spirit to God accompanies an appeal for help, not withdrawal from trouble.

Verse 15 places his “times” in God’s hand, against those who plot his end. Jesus speaks verse 5 from the cross in Luke 23:46.

chapters.title: Confession after the weight of silence
chapters.summary: The speaker calls a person blessed whose sin is forgiven and covered. While he kept silent, his bones wasted away. God’s hand was heavy on him day and night. His strength dried up as in summer heat. Then he admitted his sin and did not hide it. God forgave him. So the faithful should pray while God may be found. He tells others not to be like a mule that needs bit and bridle.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 describes hidden sin through the body. Bones waste, and groaning lasts all day. Verse 4 adds heat and a heavy hand. Verse 5 uses three verbs of opening up: acknowledge, not hide, confess. Forgiveness follows within the same verse. He had been hiding his sin; in verse 7 God becomes his hiding place. Romans 4:7–8 quotes verses 1–2.

lds.text: How does confession change the burden of silence?

chapters.historicalNote: The poem connects forgiveness with honesty. Concealment had increased the speaker’s distress.

chapters.title: Praise for the maker who sees all people
chapters.summary: The poem calls the righteous to praise the LORD with lyre and harp. The LORD’s word is right, and the earth is full of his kindness. By his word the heavens were made. He spoke, and it was done. He overturns the plans of nations, and his own plan stands. He looks from heaven and sees every person. No king is saved by a great army. The LORD’s eye is on those who hope in his kindness.
chapters.meaning: The poem first describes a world made by a word (verses 6–9). It then describes God watching every person from heaven (verses 13–15). Against that background verse 16 looks at military strength. A king’s army, a warrior’s strength, and a horse are the usual grounds of safety. Verses 16–17 say each one fails. Verse 18 names what does not fail: the LORD’s eye on those who wait. Verse 2 calls for a harp; the Egyptian harp shown is a comparison.

lds.text: What can an army fail to provide?

chapters.historicalNote: Armies and strength cannot guarantee rescue. Hope rests in the Lord’s care.

chapters.title: Learning to seek peace
chapters.summary: The heading says David acted insane before Abimelech, who sent him away. The speaker blesses the LORD, who answered him and freed him from his fears. He calls himself a poor man who cried and was heard. He invites others to taste and see that the LORD is good. He then teaches the young to fear the LORD. They should keep their tongues from evil and seek peace. The LORD is near the brokenhearted. The righteous have many troubles, and the LORD rescues them from all.
chapters.meaning: Verses 4–6 give the speaker’s own story. Verse 8 turns it into an invitation. “Taste and see” asks others to test it by experience. In verse 11 he becomes a teacher and calls the young to listen. His lesson is practical: guard speech, do good, pursue peace (verses 13–14). Verse 19 is honest that the righteous have many afflictions. First Peter 3:10–12 quotes verses 12–16.

chapters.title: A plea against false accusations
chapters.summary: The speaker asks the LORD to fight those who fight him. Without cause they hid a net for him. False witnesses accuse him and repay his good with evil. When they were sick, he wore sackcloth and fasted for them. He grieved as for a friend, a brother, or a mother. When he stumbled, they gathered to mock and tear at him. He asks how long God will look on. He promises thanks in the great assembly.
chapters.meaning: Verse 13 says the speaker fasted and prayed when these people were ill. Verse 14 says he mourned for them as for his own mother. Verse 15 gives their answer when he fell: they gathered with joy. The wound is betrayal of care he had given. The phrase “without cause” marks the poem (verses 7 and 19). He asks God to judge the matter. He does not describe taking revenge himself.

chapters.title: Wickedness and the reach of kindness
chapters.summary: The poem begins inside the mind of a wicked man. He has no fear of God and flatters himself. He plots harm even on his bed. Then the poem turns to the LORD’s kindness, which reaches the heavens. His justice is like the great mountains and the deep sea. He preserves both people and animals. People take refuge under his wings and drink from his river of delights. With him is the fountain of life.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–4 describe a small, closed world: one man scheming on his bed. Verses 5–6 open onto sky, mountains, and ocean. Verse 7 then brings that vast kindness close. People shelter under God’s wings as chicks do. The verse says “children of men,” which means humans in general. Verse 6 has already included the animals. Verses 8–9 add a feast, a river, a fountain, and light.

lds.text: How does the poem contrast deceit with the reach of kindness?

chapters.historicalNote: Human deceit appears narrow beside the wide reach of God’s protection.

chapters.title: Do not envy the success of wrongdoing
chapters.summary: This poem teaches like a proverb collection. It says not to fret over evildoers, who wither like grass. Trust the LORD, do good, and wait for him. Anger leads only to doing wrong. The humble will inherit the land. The LORD holds the hand of the one who stumbles. The speaker is old and has not seen the righteous abandoned. The wicked flourish like a green tree and then are gone.
chapters.meaning: The poem tells the reader three times not to “fret” (verses 1, 7, 8). Verse 8 says where fretting leads: to doing evil. So envy of the wicked is the real danger to the righteous. Verse 7 gives the remedy, which is to rest and wait. Verse 10 adds “a little while.” The speaker takes the long view of an old man (verse 25). Psalm 73 and the book of Job test this confidence against harder cases.

chapters.historicalNote: Its advice asks readers to choose lasting goodness over the attraction of immediate success.

chapters.title: Pain, guilt, and distant friends
chapters.summary: The speaker asks the LORD not to punish him in anger. God’s arrows have sunk into him. His body has no health, and he links this to his sin. His wounds fester, and he is bent over all day. His heart pounds, and his strength fails. Friends and neighbors keep their distance. Enemies set traps and talk of ruin. He stays silent, waits for the LORD, and asks him to hurry.
chapters.meaning: The poem has three layers of trouble. Verses 3–10 describe the body. Verse 11 says friends and relatives stand far off. Verse 12 says enemies move closer. Sickness has left him alone when he most needs company. He does not answer his accusers and leaves that to God (verses 13–15). Unlike Job he admits his sin (verse 18), and the poem ends still pleading.

lds.text: What help is missing when companions stand far away?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer joins bodily pain with guilt and loneliness. It asks God not to withdraw too.

chapters.title: The brevity of life
chapters.summary: The heading names Jeduthun. The speaker resolved to guard his mouth while the wicked were near. He kept silent, and his pain grew until his heart burned and he spoke. He asks the LORD to show him how short his life is. His days are a few handbreadths, and every person is a breath. People heap up wealth and do not know who will get it. His hope is in the LORD. He asks God to hear his tears, for he is a passing guest.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–3 describe a failed attempt at silence. The words he held in burned like fire. What finally comes out in verse 4 is a question about his own end. A handbreadth in verse 5 is the width of four fingers. It was among the smallest measures in use. Verse 6 notes that wealth is gathered for unknown heirs. In verse 12 he calls himself a stranger staying with God.

lds.text: How does a short life change the value of stored wealth?

chapters.historicalNote: Short life makes wealth uncertain. The prayer asks where hope can rest. The heading names Jeduthun in its musical directions.

contextNote.title: Guarded speech turns into a question about life
contextNote.text: Verses 1–3 describe a failed attempt at silence. The words he held in burned like fire. What finally comes out in verse 4 is a question about his own end. A handbreadth in verse 5 is the width of four fingers. It was among the smallest measures in use. Verse 6 notes that wealth is gathered for unknown heirs. In verse 12 he calls himself a stranger staying with God.

chapters.title: Rescue followed by a new appeal
chapters.summary: The speaker waited for the LORD, who heard his cry. God lifted him from a muddy pit and set his feet on rock. God put a new song in his mouth. God did not want sacrifice but an open ear. The speaker says he delights to do God’s will. He has told the great assembly of God’s faithfulness. Now troubles without number surround him again. He is poor and needy and asks God not to delay.
chapters.meaning: Most prayers of this kind move from trouble to thanks. This one runs the other way. Verses 1–10 give thanks for a rescue already received. Verses 11–17 plead in a new crisis. One rescue has not ended his need. Verse 17 calls him poor and needy, and still the Lord thinks of him. He began by waiting patiently and ends with “don’t delay.”

chapters.historicalNote: Earlier deliverance becomes a reason to pray again when new trouble arrives.

contextNote.title: A rescued voice still needs help

chapters.title: Care for the weak and betrayal
chapters.summary: The poem blesses the one who cares for the weak. The LORD sustains such a person on a sickbed. The speaker is ill and asks for mercy, since he has sinned. His enemies ask when he will die. Visitors speak empty words and gather gossip to spread. Even his close friend, who ate his bread, has turned against him. He asks God to raise him up. A blessing on the LORD closes this first part of the Psalms.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 blesses anyone who considers the weak. The speaker is now weak, and he meets the opposite. Visitors come to his bedside to collect bad news (verse 6). Verse 9 names the worst case. A trusted friend who shared his bread has turned on him. Sharing a meal was a bond of loyalty. Jesus applies this verse to Judas in John 13:18.

lds.text: What does betrayal do to the speaker’s experience of illness?

chapters.historicalNote: The kindness praised at the start contrasts with the companions’ conduct toward the suffering speaker.

contextNote.title: Illness exposes broken loyalty
contextNote.text: Verse 1 blesses anyone who considers the weak. The speaker is now weak, and he meets the opposite. Visitors come to his bedside to collect bad news (verse 6). Verse 9 names the worst case. A trusted friend who shared his bread has turned on him. Sharing a meal was a bond of loyalty. Jesus applies this verse to Judas in John 13:18.

chapters.title: Thirst for God far from worship
chapters.summary: The speaker thirsts for God as a deer pants for streams. Tears are his food while people ask where his God is. He remembers leading the crowd to God’s house with joyful songs. He asks his own soul why it is in despair. He tells it to hope in God. He is far away in the north, near Mount Hermon. Waves and breakers have gone over him. He asks God, his rock, why he has been forgotten.
chapters.meaning: Verse 5 is a refrain that returns in verse 11 and in 43:5. In it the speaker talks to himself. One part of him asks the other why it is so low. He does not deny the despair. He questions it and orders it to hope. The water pictures change through the poem. He begins with thirst (verses 1–2) and ends under a flood (verse 7).

lds.text: How can remembered worship bring both comfort and sharper grief?

chapters.historicalNote: Remembered joy deepens the sense of distance. The repeated call to hope answers inward despair. The heading names the sons of Korah.

contextNote.title: The speaker addresses his own soul
contextNote.text: Verse 5 is a refrain that returns in verse 11 and in 43:5. In it the speaker talks to himself. One part of him asks the other why it is so low. He does not deny the despair. He questions it and orders it to hope. The water pictures change through the poem. He begins with thirst (verses 1–2) and ends under a flood (verse 7).

chapters.title: Send light and truth
chapters.summary: The speaker asks God to defend him against unjust and deceitful people. God is his strength, yet he feels rejected. He asks why he must go about mourning. He asks God to send out light and truth. They will lead him to God’s holy hill. Then he will go to the altar of God, his great joy. He will praise God with the harp. He again tells his soul to hope in God.
chapters.meaning: This short poem finishes Psalm 42 and shares its refrain. Verse 3 asks for two guides: light and truth. They are pictured as an escort for a journey home. The route is named in order: hill, dwelling, altar, and God (verses 3–4). The speaker is still far away. Verse 5 repeats the question to his soul a third time. Hope is commanded, and arrival is not yet reported.

lds.text: What does the speaker ask light and truth to accomplish?

chapters.historicalNote: The repeated question to the soul connects this prayer with Psalm 42’s struggle for hope.

contextNote.title: The desired journey begins with guidance

chapters.title: A people ask why defeat came
chapters.summary: The people have heard from their fathers what God did long ago. He drove out nations and planted Israel, and their own swords did not do it. They still boast in God all day. Yet now he has rejected them and let them be defeated. They are scattered and mocked by their neighbors. All this has happened, though they have not forgotten him. They have not been false to his covenant. They cry for him to wake up and help.
chapters.meaning: This is a prayer of the whole people after a defeat. Deuteronomy 28 and the book of Judges explain defeat by unfaithfulness. Verse 17 says that explanation does not fit this time. The people claim they have kept the covenant (verses 18–21). Verse 22 says they are killed “for your sake.” Verse 23 dares to ask why God sleeps. Israel kept this protest among its songs of worship.

lds.text: Which assumption about faithful living does the people’s complaint challenge?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer questions a simple link between faithfulness and immediate success.

chapters.title: A song for a royal wedding
chapters.summary: This is a song for a king’s wedding. The poet’s heart overflows, and his tongue is like a skilled writer’s pen. He praises the king’s beauty and gracious speech. The king should ride out for truth, humility, and right. His throne lasts, and he loves what is right. His robes smell of myrrh, and music comes from ivory palaces. The poet tells the bride to forget her people and her father’s house. She is led to the king in embroidered robes with her companions.
chapters.meaning: The first half addresses the king, and verse 10 turns to the bride. The poet asks three things of her: listen, consider, and turn her ear. Then he names the cost. She must forget her people and her father’s house. The wedding is a celebration, and it is also a loss for her. Verse 16 offers sons in the place of fathers. Hebrews 1:8–9 applies verses 6–7 to Christ.

lds.text: What duties accompany the honor given to the king?

chapters.historicalNote: The wedding song joins royal honor with the demand that the king love justice.

chapters.title: Refuge when the world shakes
chapters.summary: God is the people’s refuge and strength, a help found in trouble. They will not fear though the earth gives way. Mountains may fall into the sea, and waters may roar. A river makes God’s city glad, and God is in the middle of it. Nations rage, and kingdoms totter. God speaks, and the earth melts. He ends wars, breaks the bow, and burns the chariots. He says, “Be still, and know that I am God.”
chapters.meaning: Verse 9 says God ends wars and destroys weapons. Verse 10 is his voice in that setting. “Be still” is an order to stop. It is spoken to raging nations as much as to worried worshipers. The poem sets two kinds of water side by side. The sea roars in verse 3, and a river runs quietly in verse 4. The refrain in verses 7 and 11 says the LORD of Armies is with them.

lds.text: What does stillness make possible amid the poem’s noise and danger?

chapters.historicalNote: The call to be still interrupts panic and draws attention to God’s rule.

chapters.title: Praise before the king of all nations
chapters.summary: The poem calls all peoples to clap and shout to God. The LORD Most High is a great king over all the earth. He chose an inheritance for Jacob, whom he loves. God has gone up with a shout and the sound of a trumpet. The people are told five times to sing praises. God reigns over the nations and sits on his holy throne. The princes of the peoples gather with the people of Abraham’s God.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 speaks to “all you nations,” not to Israel alone. Verse 9 pictures foreign princes assembled. They gather as the people of the God of Abraham. Genesis 12:3 promised blessing for all families through Abraham. “Shields” in this verse means rulers who protect. Verse 3 speaks of nations subdued under Israel. The poem holds both pictures, and it ends with the gathering.

lds.text: Who receives the invitation to celebrate God’s rule?

chapters.historicalNote: The praise reaches beyond Israel. The rulers of the earth belong under one greater authority.

chapters.title: Walk around Zion
chapters.summary: The LORD is great in the city of our God. Mount Zion is beautiful and is the joy of the whole earth. God has made himself known in her fortresses as a refuge. Kings gathered against her, saw her, and fled in panic. The people have heard of this, and now they have seen it. They think about God’s kindness inside his temple. They are told to walk around Zion and count her towers. They must tell the next generation that this God is their God.
chapters.meaning: Verses 12–13 send the worshipers on a tour of the walls. They count towers and study the ramparts. The purpose comes at the end of verse 13: tell the next generation. The walls are evidence for a story. Verse 3 has already said the refuge is God, not the stone. Verse 14 gives the tour’s conclusion, “this God is our God.” Verse 8 says each generation moves from hearing to seeing.

lds.text: Why should the next generation hear about the city’s protection?

chapters.historicalNote: The walk turns a visible city into a shared memory of protection.

chapters.title: Wealth cannot purchase life
chapters.summary: The poet calls all people to listen, low and high, rich and poor. He will speak wisdom and explain a riddle with the harp. He asks why he should fear when the wealthy surround him. No one can pay God a ransom for another person’s life. The wise and the foolish die alike and leave their wealth. Their graves are their homes, though they named lands after themselves. Death is their shepherd. But God will redeem the speaker’s life from the grave.
chapters.meaning: This poem speaks to all humanity, like a proverb (verses 1–2). In Israel’s law money could sometimes ransom a life (Exodus 21:30). Verse 7 says no payment works against death. Verses 8–9 call the price too high for anyone. Verse 14 pictures death as a shepherd leading his flock. Verse 15 then says what people cannot do, God will do. The refrain in verses 12 and 20 compares the proud rich to animals that perish.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects rescue from death with Jesus Christ. What does the poem say wealth cannot buy?

chapters.historicalNote: Possessions cannot redeem another person’s life. The final warning asks what riches actually secure.

chapters.title: God examines the worshipers
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. God, the LORD, calls heaven and earth as witnesses while he judges his people. He does not fault their sacrifices. But he needs no bull from their stalls, since every animal is his. If he were hungry, he would not tell them. He asks for thanks, kept vows, and prayer in trouble. He rebukes the wicked who recite his laws and join with thieves. They thought he was like them, because he kept silent.
chapters.meaning: The poem is a court scene with God as accuser and judge. Verse 8 says the offerings themselves are not the problem. The problem is the idea that God needs feeding. Verses 10–11 state that he owns every animal already. Verse 12 makes the point with dry humor. What he asks is in verses 14–15: thanks, faithfulness, and a call for help. The people need him; he does not need them.

lds.text: What separates sincere worship from using offerings to excuse harmful conduct?

chapters.historicalNote: Thanksgiving and honest conduct matter more than treating sacrifices as payment for God’s care.

chapters.title: Create a clean heart
chapters.summary: The heading sets this prayer after Nathan confronted David about Bathsheba. The speaker asks God for mercy and to blot out his wrongs. He knows his sin, and it is always before him. He asks to be washed whiter than snow. He asks God to create a clean heart in him. He asks not to be cast from God’s presence. Then he will teach other wrongdoers God’s ways. God wants a broken and humble heart more than a burnt offering.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–2 and 9 ask God to blot out a record. Verse 10 asks for more than a cleared account. “Create” is the word used for God’s work in Genesis 1:1. The speaker cannot make a clean heart for himself. He asks God to make one. Verse 11 fears losing God’s Spirit, as Saul did (1 Samuel 16:14). Verse 13 expects a forgiven man to become a teacher.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies forgiveness and a renewed heart. What changes does the speaker ask God to make?

chapters.historicalNote: The request reaches beyond escape from punishment toward a changed heart. The heading recalls Nathan visiting David after his conduct toward Bathsheba.

contextNote.title: Confession asks for more than erased guilt

chapters.title: A powerful person’s harmful words
chapters.summary: The heading names Doeg, who told Saul that David went to Ahimelech’s house. The speaker asks a powerful man why he boasts of evil. His tongue is like a sharp razor and loves lies. God will tear him from his tent and uproot him from the living. The righteous will see it and laugh. That man trusted his great wealth and not God. The speaker is like a green olive tree in God’s house. He trusts God’s kindness and gives thanks.
chapters.meaning: Verse 5 says the boaster will be uprooted. Verse 8 answers with a tree that stays rooted. An olive tree is evergreen and lives for many generations. This one grows in God’s house. Verse 7 says the powerful man trusted in riches. The speaker trusts in loving kindness. First Samuel 22:9–19 shows what Doeg’s tongue cost the priests of Nob.

lds.text: How do destructive words expose the powerful person’s trust?

chapters.historicalNote: Destructive speech exposes misplaced confidence. The living tree represents trust in enduring kindness. The heading recalls Doeg telling Saul about David’s visit to Ahimelech.

chapters.title: Corruption and rescue for Israel
chapters.summary: This poem is nearly the same as Psalm 14. The fool says in his heart that there is no God. People are corrupt, and no one does good. God looks down to see whether anyone seeks him. Everyone has turned away. Evildoers eat up God’s people like bread and never call on him. Then great terror falls on them where no terror was. The speaker longs for Israel’s rescue to come from Zion.
chapters.meaning: The book keeps this poem twice, here with the name “God” throughout. Verse 4 holds the charge. The evildoers consume people as an everyday meal. They also do not call on God. Verse 5 is the main difference from Psalm 14. Panic strikes the oppressors when nothing threatens them. The people they frightened are not the ones who end in fear.

lds.text: Why does the closing hope look beyond human strength?

chapters.historicalNote: Its closing hope seeks the restoration of Israel rather than praising human strength.

chapters.title: Help against strangers and violent people
chapters.summary: The heading says men of Ziph told Saul where David was hiding. The speaker asks God to save him by his name. Strangers have risen against him, and violent men want his life. They do not keep God before them. Then he says that God is his helper. The Lord sustains his life. He will bring a freewill offering and give thanks. God has rescued him from every trouble.
chapters.meaning: This prayer has seven verses, and verse 4 is its hinge. Before it the speaker pleads. After it he speaks as if the rescue were done. Verse 3 says his enemies have not set God before them. In verse 4 he does exactly that with the word “Behold.” Nothing outward has changed between verses 3 and 4. First Samuel 23:19 tells of the betrayal the heading names.

lds.text: What kind of support does the speaker ask God to provide?

chapters.historicalNote: The heading connects the prayer with the Ziphites reporting David’s hiding place to Saul.

chapters.title: Betrayal by a close companion
chapters.summary: The speaker asks God not to hide from his plea. His heart is in anguish, and the terrors of death have fallen on him. He wishes for a dove’s wings to fly away and rest. He sees violence, strife, and fraud in the city. An enemy’s insult he could have borne. But this was his equal, his companion and close friend. They used to walk together to God’s house. He tells himself to cast his burden on the LORD.
chapters.meaning: Verse 12 says he could have endured an enemy or hidden from one. Verse 13 names the real source: “a man like me.” The friend was his equal and knew him well. Verse 14 adds that they worshiped together. This kind of harm makes him want to flee, not fight (verses 6–8). Verse 21 describes speech as smooth as butter that hides a sword. Verse 22 promises he will be sustained, not that the burden goes.

lds.text: Why does betrayal by a trusted companion differ from an enemy’s attack?

chapters.historicalNote: Shared worship makes the betrayal especially painful. The prayer seeks support beyond the failed friendship.

contextNote.title: The deepest threat comes from a companion

chapters.title: Trust amid fear
chapters.summary: The heading says the Philistines seized David in Gath. The speaker asks for mercy, since men attack him all day. When he is afraid, he puts his trust in God. He asks what mere flesh can do to him. His enemies twist his words and watch his steps. He says God has counted his wanderings. God keeps his tears in a bottle and writes them in a book. He knows that God is for him.
chapters.meaning: Verse 6 says enemies mark the speaker’s steps in order to kill him. Verse 8 says God also keeps count of his wanderings. The same watching has an opposite purpose. God stores his tears and records them. Nothing he suffers is lost or overlooked. Verse 3 does not deny fear: “When I am afraid.” Verse 9 gives his conclusion: God is for him.

lds.text: How does the speaker acknowledge fear before expressing trust?

chapters.historicalNote: Fear is admitted before trust is expressed. The poem treats tears as worth remembering.

contextNote.title: Tears become a request for remembrance

chapters.title: Shelter until danger passes
chapters.summary: The heading sets this prayer in the cave where David hid from Saul. The speaker asks for mercy and shelters under God’s wings. He will stay there until the danger passes. He lies among lions whose teeth are spears. He asks God to be exalted above the heavens. His enemies dug a pit and fell into it themselves. His heart is steady, and he will sing. He will wake the dawn with harp and lyre.
chapters.meaning: Verse 6 turns in the middle. The enemies spread a net and dig a pit. Then they fall into it themselves. The poem pauses there. The refrain in verses 5 and 11 lifts the view above the cave. In verse 8 the speaker does not wait for morning. He says he will wake the dawn with his song.

lds.text: What changes when the speaker turns from describing traps to praise?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer moves from danger toward praise without pretending the threats were harmless.

chapters.title: A cry against unjust rulers
chapters.summary: The speaker asks rulers whether they really speak justice. He says their hearts plan wrong and their hands deal out violence. The wicked go astray from birth. Their poison is like a cobra’s that hears no charmer. He asks God to break their teeth. He asks that they vanish like water that runs off. The righteous will be glad when they see justice done. People will say there is a God who judges the earth.
chapters.meaning: The poem speaks to people whose work is to judge. Verse 2 says they “measure out” violence. A judge should weigh evidence, and these weigh out harm. The curses in verses 6–9 are fierce. They are requests handed to God; they are not actions taken. Verse 11 gives the reason for them. People need to be able to say that someone judges the earth.

lds.text: What injustice produces the speaker’s forceful anger?

chapters.historicalNote: The harsh images express anger at injustice. They show the force of the speaker’s demand.

contextNote.title: The prayer challenges corrupt judgment
contextNote.text: The poem speaks to people whose work is to judge. Verse 2 says they “measure out” violence. A judge should weigh evidence, and these weigh out harm. chapters.title: Enemies circle the house
chapters.summary: The heading says Saul sent men to watch David’s house and kill him. The speaker asks God to rescue him from men who lie in wait. He has done no wrong to them. They return at evening, howl like dogs, and prowl the city. They think no one hears. The LORD laughs at them. The speaker asks God to scatter them but not to kill them. In the morning he will sing of God’s strength.
chapters.meaning: Two refrains shape this poem. Verses 6 and 14 describe the enemies as dogs prowling at evening. Verses 9 and 17 call God “my strength.” The evening belongs to the enemies. Verse 16 gives the morning to the speaker’s song. Verse 11 makes an unusual request. He wants them left alive, so that his people do not forget.

lds.text: How does the repeated picture of prowling dogs increase the sense of danger?

chapters.historicalNote: The heading connects the threat with Saul’s men watching David’s house.

contextNote.title: Repeated sounds organize the danger
contextNote.text: Two refrains shape this poem. Verses 6 and 14 describe the enemies as dogs prowling at evening. Verses 9 and 17 call God “my strength.” The evening belongs to the enemies. Verse 16 gives the morning to the speaker’s song. Verse 11 makes an unusual request. He wants them left alive, so that his people do not forget.

chapters.title: Defeat and a renewed appeal
chapters.summary: The heading sets this prayer when David fought Aram and Joab struck Edom. The people say God has rejected them and broken their defenses. He has shaken the land and made them stagger. They ask him to save with his right hand. God has spoken: Shechem, Gilead, Ephraim, and Judah are his. Moab, Edom, and Philistia are under him. Yet God has not gone out with their armies. They ask for his help, since human help is worthless.
chapters.meaning: Verses 6–8 quote God claiming every region by name. Verse 10 sets a recent defeat against that claim. God has not gone out with the armies. The people hold the promise and the loss together. They do not drop either one. Verse 11 draws the lesson that human help is empty. Verse 12 still expects victory through God.

lds.text: Why does the people’s defeat lead to a renewed appeal?

chapters.historicalNote: The named lands appear in a plea for renewed strength, not a travel account. The heading names Joab in a remembered battle against Edom.

contextNote.title: Defeat creates a question about divine presence
contextNote.text: Verses 6–8 quote God claiming every region by name. Verse 10 sets a recent defeat against that claim. God has not gone out with the armies. The people hold the promise and the loss together. They do not drop either one. Verse 11 draws the lesson that human help is empty. Verse 12 still expects victory through God.

chapters.title: A prayer from far away
chapters.summary: The speaker asks God to hear his cry. He calls from the end of the earth with a fainting heart. He asks to be led to a rock higher than himself. God has been his refuge and a strong tower. He wants to live in God’s tent and shelter under his wings. God has heard his vows. He prays for long life for the king. He will sing and keep his vows day after day.
chapters.meaning: Verse 2 places the speaker at “the end of the earth.” He is far from God’s house, or feels that he is. He asks for a rock “higher than I.” It is a height he cannot reach alone, so he says, “Lead me.” Verse 3 gives his reason for asking. God has been a refuge to him before. Verses 6–7 add a prayer for the king.

lds.text: What does shelter mean to someone who feels far away?

chapters.historicalNote: Distance becomes a reason to seek a refuge stronger than the speaker’s own position.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: Distance shapes the request for refuge
contextNote.text: Verse 2 places the speaker at “the end of the earth.” He is far from God’s house, or feels that he is. He asks for a rock “higher than I.” It is a height he cannot reach alone, so he says, “Lead me.” Verse 3 gives his reason for asking. God has been a refuge to him before. Verses 6–7 add a prayer for the king.

chapters.title: Waiting without depending on riches
chapters.summary: The heading names Jeduthun. The speaker waits in silence for God alone, his rock and fortress. Men attack him like a leaning wall and bless with their mouths while cursing inside. He tells his soul again to wait. He tells the people to trust God and pour out their hearts. Human beings of every rank weigh less than a breath. They should not trust in extortion or set their hearts on wealth. Power and kindness both belong to God.
chapters.meaning: The word “alone” or “only” runs through verses 1, 2, 5, and 6. Verse 9 removes people of every rank as a support. Verse 10 removes money gained by force or theft. It then adds a harder case. Even if riches simply grow, the heart must not settle on them. Wealth is not condemned, and trust in it is. Verses 11–12 name what remains: God’s power joined with kindness.

chapters.historicalNote: Silence expresses settled reliance. The poem joins power with kindness and accountability.

chapters.title: Longing for God in dry land
chapters.summary: The heading sets this prayer in the wilderness of Judah. The speaker thirsts for God in a dry and weary land. He has seen God’s power in the sanctuary. God’s kindness is better than life. His soul is satisfied as with the richest food. He remembers God on his bed through the night watches. He clings to God, whose right hand holds him. Those who seek his life will fall, and the king will rejoice.
chapters.meaning: The night was divided into watches for guards. Verse 6 says the speaker lies awake through them, thinking of God. His thirst in verse 1 is met by memory in verse 2. Verse 5 says he is satisfied as with a feast, in a desert. Verse 3 values God’s kindness above life itself. Verse 8 describes holding in both directions. He clings, and God’s hand holds him up.

lds.text: What does the speaker remember during the night?

chapters.historicalNote: Dry land gives a physical image to longing. Memory sustains praise while the need remains.

contextNote.title: Thirst continues through the night
contextNote.text: The night was divided into watches for guards. Verse 6 says the speaker lies awake through them, thinking of God. His thirst in verse 1 is met by memory in verse 2. Verse 5 says he is satisfied as with a feast, in a desert. Verse 3 values God’s kindness above life itself. Verse 8 describes holding in both directions. He clings, and God’s hand holds him up.

chapters.title: Hidden plots and harmful speech
chapters.summary: The speaker asks God to hear his complaint and guard his life. The wicked plot in secret. They sharpen their tongues like swords and aim bitter words like arrows. They shoot from hiding at the innocent. They encourage one another and ask who will see them. God will shoot his own arrow at them suddenly. Their own tongues will bring them down. Everyone will fear and tell what God has done.
chapters.meaning: The weapons in verse 3 are words. The attack is secret, sudden, and sure it is unseen (verses 2, 4, 5). The poem treats slander as seriously as violence. Verse 7 answers in the same terms. God shoots an arrow, and it also comes “suddenly.” Verse 8 says their own tongues will ruin them. The harm returns by the road it came.

chapters.historicalNote: The poem expects hidden attacks to become visible through God’s judgment.

chapters.title: Praise for forgiveness and harvest
chapters.summary: Praise waits for God in Zion. He hears prayer, and all people come to him. He forgives the sins that overwhelm them. He set the mountains in place and stills the roaring seas. He visits the earth and waters it. He drenches the furrows and softens the ground with showers. He crowns the year with goodness. The pastures and valleys are covered with flocks and grain, and they sing.
chapters.meaning: The poem moves in three parts. Verses 1–4 stand in the temple, and verses 5–8 view mountains and seas. Verses 9–13 walk through farmland. Verse 9 pictures God as a farmer visiting his field. He waters it and prepares the grain. Verse 10 follows the rain into the plowed furrows. In verse 13 the land itself shouts and sings.

lds.text: How does care for the land enter the people’s praise?

chapters.historicalNote: Care for the land connects worship with the food that sustains ordinary life.

chapters.title: A people remember rescue
chapters.summary: The poem calls all the earth to shout to God. People are invited to come and see what he has done. He turned the sea into dry land. He tested his people and refined them like silver. They went through fire and water, and he brought them to a rich place. Then one voice speaks. He will pay the vows he made in distress. He tells all who fear God what God has done for him.
chapters.meaning: The poem changes speaker at verse 13. Verses 1–12 say “we” and tell the nation’s story. Verses 13–20 say “I.” Verse 5 invites people to “come and see” the great acts of old. Verse 16 invites them to “come and hear” one person’s account. A single life is set beside the crossing of the sea. Verse 18 adds that he did not hold on to wrong in his heart.

chapters.title: Blessing that reaches the nations
chapters.summary: The people ask God to be merciful, bless them, and shine his face on them. They ask this so that his way may be known on earth. All nations should know his salvation. The peoples are called to praise God and be glad. He judges them fairly and guides them. The earth has given its harvest. God blesses his people, and all the ends of the earth will fear him.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 borrows the priests’ blessing from Numbers 6:24–26. Verse 2 adds a purpose to it with the word “that.” Israel asks to be blessed so that others may know God’s way. The blessing is not meant to stop with those who receive it. The refrain in verses 3 and 5 names “all the peoples.” Verse 6 suggests a harvest as the occasion. The last verse reaches to the ends of the earth.

chapters.title: The protector leads his people
chapters.summary: God rises, and his enemies scatter like smoke. The righteous sing to the one who rides through the deserts. He is a father to orphans and a defender of widows. He gives the lonely a home and leads prisoners out. He marched before his people, and Sinai shook. Kings and armies flee. A procession of singers, musicians, and young women enters the sanctuary. Kings bring gifts, and God gives strength to his people.
chapters.meaning: This is a poem of marching, battle, and procession. Verse 5 says what kind of ruler leads it. In his holy dwelling God is father to the fatherless. He defends widows, who had no one to speak for them. Verse 6 adds homes for the lonely and freedom for prisoners. The poem describes God’s power by naming those it protects. Verse 1 repeats the words spoken when the ark set out (Numbers 10:35).

chapters.historicalNote: Praise connects great power with care for orphans, widows, and prisoners.

chapters.title: Sinking beneath shame and hostility
chapters.summary: The speaker cries that the waters have reached his neck. He sinks in deep mud, and his throat is dry from calling. Many hate him without cause. He bears insult for God’s sake and is a stranger to his brothers. People at the gate talk about him, and drunkards sing about him. Insult has broken his heart. He looked for pity and found none. He asks God to answer, and he promises a song of thanks.
chapters.meaning: The poem opens with drowning, but its deepest wound is shame. Verses 7–12 describe mockery from family, elders, and drunkards. Verse 20 says insult has broken his heart. He looked for comforters and found none, as Job did. Verse 21 shows the only “care” he received: gall and vinegar. The curses in verses 22–28 are handed to God. The Gospels apply verses 9 and 21 to Jesus (John 2:17; Matthew 27:34).

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer gives voice to isolation and anger. Its demands against enemies require careful reading.

contextNote.title: Ridicule makes suffering publicly visible

chapters.title: An urgent call for help
chapters.summary: This short prayer asks God to hurry. The speaker wants those who seek his life to be put to shame. He wants those who mock him turned back. He wants all who seek God to rejoice and say that God is great. He is poor and needy. He asks God to come quickly. God is his help and rescuer, and he asks him not to delay.
chapters.meaning: The prayer has only five verses. It begins with “hurry” and ends with “don’t delay.” Verses 3 and 4 divide people by what they say. One group says, “Aha!” The other says, “Let God be exalted.” The speaker has no time for a longer form. These verses also appear at the end of Psalm 40.

lds.text: Why is delay especially difficult for this speaker?

chapters.historicalNote: The short prayer keeps urgency at its center. The speaker has no resources to delay.

contextNote.title: Urgency supplies the poem’s structure

chapters.title: A prayer in old age
chapters.summary: The speaker takes refuge in the LORD and asks for rescue. God has been his hope since his youth. He has leaned on God from birth. He asks not to be cast off in old age when his strength fails. His enemies say God has left him. He will still hope and tell of God’s saving acts all day. He asks to live until he has told the next generation. He will praise God with harp and lyre.
chapters.meaning: The speaker names the womb, youth, and gray hair (verses 6, 17, 18). His enemies read his weakness as proof that God has gone (verses 10–11). Verse 18 gives his reason for wanting more time. He has not finished telling the next generation. Verse 20 admits that God let him see many troubles. Verse 22 promises music on the harp and lyre. The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison, not Israel’s instrument.

lds.text: What can the speaker still give the next generation in old age?

chapters.historicalNote: Old age becomes a time to tell the next generation about God’s help.

chapters.title: A king who protects the poor
chapters.summary: This is a prayer for the king. The people ask God to give him justice. He should defend the poor, save needy children, and crush the oppressor. May he be like rain on a mown field. May he rule from sea to sea and receive gifts from distant kings. He rescues the needy who cry out and have no helper. Their blood is precious to him. May all nations be blessed through him.
chapters.meaning: Verses 8–11 pray for a rule that reaches the ends of the earth. Verse 12 begins with “For” and gives the reason. This king deserves such rule because he rescues the helpless. Verse 14 says their blood is precious in his sight. Their deaths matter to him. The prayer describes an ideal that no king in the Bible’s history fully met. In 1 Kings 12:4 the people call Solomon’s own rule a heavy yoke.

lds.text: How does protection of the poor measure the quality of a ruler?

chapters.historicalNote: Good rule receives its measure from the safety of those who lack power. The heading names Solomon.

contextNote.title: Royal greatness is measured through vulnerable lives

chapters.title: Envy challenged in the sanctuary
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The speaker says God is good to the pure in heart. Yet his feet almost slipped when he envied the arrogant and saw them prosper. They have no pain, wear pride like a necklace, and mock heaven. He wondered whether he had kept his heart clean for nothing. The problem wore him out until he entered God’s sanctuary. There he understood their end. He says God holds his hand and is his portion forever.
chapters.meaning: Nothing in the speaker’s circumstances changes at verse 17. Two things change. He stands in a different place, the sanctuary. He looks at a different time, the “end” of the wicked. In verse 15 he says he kept silent to protect others. In verses 21–22 he admits his own bitterness. His answer is finally a presence and not an explanation (verses 23–26).

lds.text: What changes when the speaker enters the sanctuary?

chapters.historicalNote: The poem admits the attraction of easy success before finding a different measure of good. The heading names Asaph.

contextNote.title: A changed perspective answers envy

In verse 15 he says he kept silent to protect others. In verses 21–22 he admits his own bitterness. His answer is finally a presence and not an explanation (verses 23–26).

chapters.title: A plea after the sanctuary’s destruction
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The people ask God why he has rejected them. Enemies have ruined everything in the sanctuary. They hacked the carved wood with axes and burned the holy place. They burned every meeting place in the land. No signs are seen, no prophet remains, and no one knows how long. The people recall that God divided the sea and crushed the sea monsters. They ask him to remember his covenant and defend his cause.
chapters.meaning: The poem fits the burning of the temple in 2 Kings 25:9. Verse 9 lists three losses beyond the building. There are no signs, no prophet, and no one who knows how long. The people have lost their guidance. Verse 4 says the enemy set up their own signs there. The people answer by remembering something older than the temple. Verses 12–17 recall God’s power over sea, day, and season.

lds.text: What has the destruction taken from the people beyond a building?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer joins damaged buildings with the fear that God has withdrawn from the community.

contextNote.title: Ruined worship removes familiar guidance
contextNote.text: The poem fits the burning of the temple in 2 Kings 25:9. Verse 9 lists three losses beyond the building. There are no signs, no prophet, and no one who knows how long. The people have lost their guidance. Verse 4 says the enemy set up their own signs there. The people answer by remembering something older than the temple. Verses 12–17 recall God’s power over sea, day, and season.

chapters.title: A warning against proud power
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The people thank God, whose name is near. God says he will judge at his chosen time and holds the earth’s pillars steady. He tells the proud not to boast or lift up their strength. Honor does not come from east, west, or the desert. God is the judge, who puts one down and lifts another up. He holds a cup of foaming wine for the wicked. The speaker will sing praise to the God of Jacob.
chapters.meaning: The idea of “lifting up” runs through verses 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10. The proud lift up their own horn, a picture of an animal’s strength. Verse 6 says promotion comes from no point on the map. Verse 7 gives the true source. God is the judge who lowers and raises. Verse 2 adds that he also sets the time. The boasters control neither the outcome nor the hour.

lds.text: What claims to power does the raised-horn image challenge?

chapters.historicalNote: Raised horns picture claims to strength. The warning challenges power that refuses restraint.

contextNote.title: Judgment interrupts boasting

Verse 6 says promotion comes from no point on the map. Verse 7 gives the true source. God is the judge who lowers and raises. Verse 2 adds that he also sets the time. The boasters control neither the outcome nor the hour.

chapters.title: God stops the weapons of war
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. God is known in Judah, and his dwelling is in Zion. There he broke the flaming arrows, the shield, and the sword. Brave soldiers lay stunned, and at his rebuke horse and chariot fell still. No one can stand when he is angry. The earth feared and was quiet when God rose to judge. He rose to save all the afflicted of the earth. Rulers should bring gifts to the one who humbles princes.
chapters.meaning: Verses 3–8 describe a power that stops armies. Verse 3 says God broke the weapons themselves. Verse 8 says the whole earth fell silent. Verse 9 gives the purpose of that power. God rose to judge in order to save the afflicted. The verse says “of the earth,” so the afflicted of every land are meant. The poem celebrates the end of a battle, not the fighting.

lds.text: Who gains protection when the weapons lose their force?

chapters.historicalNote: Divine judgment protects the afflicted while ending the confidence of armed power.

contextNote.title: Broken weapons explain the celebrated power
contextNote.text: Verses 3–8 describe a power that stops armies. Verse 3 says God broke the weapons themselves. Verse 8 says the whole earth fell silent. Verse 9 gives the purpose of that power. God rose to judge in order to save the afflicted. The verse says “of the earth,” so the afflicted of every land are meant. The poem celebrates the end of a battle, not the fighting.

chapters.title: Remembering rescue during a sleepless night
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph and Jeduthun. The speaker cries aloud to God in the day of trouble. At night he finds no comfort, and he cannot sleep or speak. He asks whether the Lord will reject forever and whether his kindness has ended. Then he decides to remember the LORD’s deeds of old. God redeemed the children of Jacob and Joseph. The waters saw him and trembled. He led his people through the sea like a flock.
chapters.meaning: Verses 7–9 ask six questions, and none is answered directly. In verse 11 the speaker chooses to remember the exodus. Verse 19 holds the key thought. God made a path through the sea, yet his footprints were not seen. He acted and left no visible track. So a night with no trace of God does not prove he is gone. The poem ends with the flock being led (verse 20).

lds.text: How does remembering the sea crossing answer a sleepless night?

chapters.historicalNote: Memory does not erase the questions. It provides another way to see the present silence.

contextNote.title: Memory answers an unanswered night
contextNote.text: Verses 7–9 ask six questions, and none is answered directly. In verse 11 the speaker chooses to remember the exodus. Verse 19 holds the key thought. The poem ends with the flock being led (verse 20).

chapters.title: Tell the children about earlier failures
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The poet asks the people to listen, for fathers must tell children the LORD’s deeds. Then each generation will hope in God and not be stubborn. He recalls the sea, the cloud, water from the rock, and manna. The people still tested God and forgot his works. God was merciful and remembered that they were only flesh. He left Shiloh and let the ark be captured. He chose Judah, Mount Zion, and David the shepherd.
chapters.meaning: Verses 5–6 describe a chain of four generations. Fathers teach children, who teach children not yet born. The lesson they pass on includes Israel’s failures. Verse 8 gives the aim: that they not be like their fathers. History is told here as a warning, not a boast. Verse 7 names three hoped results: hope, memory, and obedience. The long story ends with a shepherd chosen to lead (verses 70–72).

lds.text: What should children learn from the failures described?

chapters.historicalNote: The long account asks the next generation to learn rather than repeat the same failures.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: History becomes instruction for children
contextNote.text: Verses 5–6 describe a chain of four generations. Fathers teach children, who teach children not yet born. The lesson they pass on includes Israel’s failures. Verse 8 gives the aim: that they not be like their fathers. History is told here as a warning, not a boast. Verse 7 names three hoped results: hope, memory, and obedience. The long story ends with a shepherd chosen to lead (verses 70–72).

chapters.title: Prayer among the ruins of Jerusalem
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The nations have invaded God’s land, defiled his temple, and left Jerusalem in ruins. The bodies of God’s servants are left for birds and animals. Neighbors mock the survivors. The people ask how long God will be angry. They ask him not to hold their earlier sins against them. They ask for help and forgiveness for the sake of his name. Then his people, his flock, will thank him forever.
chapters.meaning: Unlike Psalm 44, this prayer admits the people’s sins (verses 8–9). Verse 9 names the ground of their appeal twice. They ask for the glory of God’s name and for his name’s sake. Verse 10 shows what is at stake: nations ask where their God is. So they ask for rescue as mercy and as a defense of God’s honor. Verses 2–3 describe the dead left unburied. That was a deep disgrace.

lds.text: Why do the people ask for forgiveness as well as rescue?

chapters.historicalNote: Grief leads to requests for forgiveness, rescue, and judgment against those who caused the destruction.

contextNote.title: A shattered community appeals through God’s name
contextNote.text: Unlike Psalm 44, this prayer admits the people’s sins (verses 8–9). Verse 9 names the ground of their appeal twice. They ask for the glory of God’s name and for his name’s sake. Verse 10 shows what is at stake: nations ask where their God is. So they ask for rescue as mercy and as a defense of God’s honor. Verses 2–3 describe the dead left unburied. That was a deep disgrace.

chapters.title: Restore the vine you brought from Egypt
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The people call on the Shepherd of Israel to shine and save them. Three times they ask God to restore them and let his face shine. He has fed them with tears. They recall that God brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it. It filled the land and shaded the mountains. Now its walls are broken, passersby pick its fruit, and a wild boar tears it. They ask God to look down and care for this vine.
chapters.meaning: Verses 8–11 tell Israel’s story as a transplanted vine that flourished. Verse 12 asks why God himself broke down its wall. The gardener has left his own work open to animals. Verse 14 asks him to turn, look, and tend it again. The refrain grows each time it returns (verses 3, 7, 19). God’s title becomes longer and fuller. Isaiah 5:1–7 uses the same picture and gives a reason for the ruin.

lds.text: How do the vine’s broken walls picture a people open to attack?

chapters.historicalNote: The vine once spread widely. Its broken defenses picture a people exposed to attack.

contextNote.title: A vine gives collective loss a form
contextNote.text: Verses 8–11 tell Israel’s story as a transplanted vine that flourished. Verse 12 asks why God himself broke down its wall. The gardener has left his own work open to animals. Verse 14 asks him to turn, look, and tend it again. The refrain grows each time it returns (verses 3, 7, 19). God’s title becomes longer and fuller. Isaiah 5:1–7 uses the same picture and gives a reason for the ruin.

chapters.title: Listen to the voice that freed you
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The poem opens with a call to sing and play at the festival. Trumpets sound at the new moon, as Israel’s law requires, and then God speaks. He lifted the burden from Israel’s shoulder in Egypt. He tells his people to have no foreign god. He brought them out of Egypt and will fill their open mouths. But the people would not listen, so he let them follow their own plans. If they would listen, he would feed them with the finest wheat.
chapters.meaning: Festival music fills verses 1–3. From verse 6 God’s own voice interrupts it. Verses 9–10 repeat the opening of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2–3). “Open your mouth wide” pictures a young bird waiting to be fed. Verses 11–12 give the sad result. The people’s penalty is to get their own way. Verse 13 begins “Oh that,” which is God’s own longing.

lds.text: What response should follow the memory of release from slavery?

chapters.historicalNote: The warning says freedom should lead to listening rather than continued refusal.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: Festival praise becomes an appeal to listen
contextNote.text: Festival music fills verses 1–3. From verse 6 God’s own voice interrupts it. Verses 9–10 repeat the opening of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2–3). “Open your mouth wide” pictures a young bird waiting to be fed. Verses 11–12 give the sad result. The people’s penalty is to get their own way. Verse 13 begins “Oh that,” which is God’s own longing.

chapters.title: God judges the assembly
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. God stands in the assembly and judges among the “gods.” He asks how long they will judge unjustly and favor the wicked. He orders them to defend the weak and the fatherless. They must rescue the poor from the wicked. They walk in darkness, and the earth’s foundations shake. God says they will die like men. The poet asks God to rise and judge the earth, since all nations are his.
chapters.meaning: Readers differ on who the “gods” are. Some see heavenly beings, and others see human judges. Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10:34. Either way, verse 3 states the test of a ruler. He must defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Verse 5 says their failure shakes the foundations of the earth. Verse 8 asks God to take the work over himself.

lds.text: What duties have the accused figures failed to fulfill?

chapters.historicalNote: McClellan reads the accused figures as other gods failing to govern their nations justly.

contextNote.title: A heavenly courtroom examines earthly injustice
contextNote.text: Readers differ on who the “gods” are. Some see heavenly beings, and others see human judges. Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10:34. Either way, verse 3 states the test of a ruler. He must defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Verse 5 says their failure shakes the foundations of the earth. Verse 8 asks God to take the work over himself.

chapters.title: A prayer against surrounding enemies
chapters.summary: The heading names Asaph. The people ask God not to stay silent. Enemies are plotting to wipe out Israel’s name. Ten peoples have joined together, from Edom and Moab to Tyre and Assyria. The people ask God to treat them as he treated Midian and Sisera. They ask that the enemies be like windblown dust and their faces filled with shame. Then they may seek his name. Let them know that the LORD alone is Most High.
chapters.meaning: Verses 6–8 list ten peoples surrounding Israel. Verse 4 states their aim: to erase a nation’s name. Verse 16 states the aim of the prayer. Shame should lead the enemies to seek God’s name. Verse 18 asks that they come to know who he is. Verse 17 still asks for their ruin, and the poem keeps both requests. Even this war prayer hopes its enemies will recognize God.

lds.text: How do remembered victories shape the request against present enemies?

chapters.historicalNote: Memories of earlier victories become the language for a present plea for protection.

chapters.title: Longing for God’s courts
chapters.summary: The speaker loves the LORD’s dwelling and longs for its courts. Even the sparrow and the swallow have nests near God’s altars. Those who live in God’s house are blessed. So are those who set their hearts on the road to Zion. They pass through a dry valley and make it a place of springs. A day in God’s courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. The speaker would choose to be a doorkeeper there. The LORD is a sun and shield.
chapters.meaning: The heading gives this poem to the sons of Korah. First Chronicles 9:19 says that family kept the temple gates. So “doorkeeper” in verse 10 is their own post. The lowest job in God’s house is better than a home among the wicked. Verse 3 envies birds that nest near the altar. Verses 5–7 follow travelers on the road there. The verse measures a place by who is present in it.

lds.text: Why does the speaker want even one day near the altar?

chapters.historicalNote: The journey’s hardship stands beside the desire for one day near God.

chapters.title: A people ask for renewed life
chapters.summary: The people recall that the LORD once restored and forgave them. They ask him to restore them again. They ask whether he will be angry forever. The speaker will listen for what God says. God speaks peace to his people, and they must not return to folly. Mercy and truth meet. Righteousness and peace kiss each other. The LORD will give what is good, and the land will yield its harvest.
chapters.meaning: The poem moves from past favor to a present plea to listening (verses 1–8). Verses 9–13 describe what the speaker hears. Verse 10 pictures four qualities as people meeting on a road. These often pull apart in human experience. Truth can lack mercy, and peace can ignore what is right. Here they greet each other. Verse 11 adds truth rising from the earth as righteousness looks down.

lds.text: How does the poem connect peace with justice?

chapters.historicalNote: Peace includes justice. The poem joins renewed life with a changed relationship to God.

chapters.title: A plea from a faithful servant
chapters.summary: The speaker is poor and needy and asks the LORD to hear him. God is good, forgiving, and full of kindness to all who call. No god is like him. All nations he made will come and worship. The speaker asks to be taught God’s way. He asks for an undivided heart. Proud and violent men seek his life. He calls God merciful and gracious and asks for a sign of favor.
chapters.meaning: Most of the prayer asks for rescue. Verse 11 asks for something inside the speaker. He wants to be taught, and he wants one heart. A heart pulled several ways cannot fear God’s name. Verse 12 then promises thanks “with my whole heart.” Verse 15 quotes God’s own description of himself in Exodus 34:6. The speaker’s request rests on that character.

lds.text: What would an undivided heart change about the speaker’s choices?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer links rescue with learning to walk in God’s truth.
