chapters.title: Peoples counted as belonging to Zion
chapters.summary: The LORD loves the gates of Zion, and glorious things are said of the city. God lists nations among those who know him. He names Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia. Of each one it is said, “This one was born there.” The Most High himself will establish Zion. When he registers the peoples, he records them as born in her. Singers and dancers say all their springs are in her.
chapters.meaning: The nations named in verse 4 include Israel’s old enemies. “Rahab” there is a name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7). Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, and Philistia fought it for generations. Verse 5 says such people are counted as born in Zion. Verse 6 shows God writing the register himself. Belonging rests on his record, not on birthplace. The poem makes a city’s citizens out of its former foes.

lds.text: How does counting people from other nations as born in Zion change who belongs?

chapters.historicalNote: The birth register widens belonging beyond one people’s ancestry. Rahab here names Egypt poetically.

chapters.title: A prayer that ends in darkness
chapters.summary: The heading names the sons of Korah and Heman the Ezrahite. The speaker cries to the LORD day and night. His life is full of trouble and close to the grave. He is counted among the dead whom God remembers no more. God’s anger lies heavy on him. He asks whether God works wonders for the dead. He has been afflicted since his youth. Friend and neighbor are gone, and darkness is his companion.
chapters.meaning: This is the one prayer in the book with no turn toward hope. Its last word is “darkness.” Yet verse 1 calls the LORD “the God of my salvation.” The speaker says three times that he keeps praying (verses 1, 9, 13). His faith shows in the fact that he still speaks. The book of Psalms includes this prayer with the rest. A person may pray this way and still be praying.

lds.text: What does the prayer preserve by ending without relief?

chapters.historicalNote: The final line offers no turn toward relief. The prayer preserves suffering without a quick resolution. The heading names Heman the Ezrahite and the sons of Korah.

contextNote.title: Some prayers end without visible relief

chapters.title: A promise to David amid royal defeat
chapters.summary: The heading names Ethan the Ezrahite. The poet sings of the LORD’s kindness and faithfulness. God swore that David’s line and throne would last forever. The heavens praise him, and justice is the base of his throne. If David’s sons sin, God will punish them and still keep his kindness. Then the poem turns. God has rejected his anointed and thrown the crown in the dust. Walls are broken, enemies rejoice, and the poet asks where the former kindness is.
chapters.meaning: For thirty-seven verses the poet praises a sworn promise. Verse 38 begins, “But you have rejected.” He quotes God’s oath and sets the facts beside it (verses 34–35, 39–45). Verse 49 asks where the sworn kindness has gone. He complains because he believes the promise. The poem gives no answer. A blessing in verse 52 closes the third part of the Psalms.

lds.text: How does the broken crown challenge the people’s understanding of a lasting promise?

chapters.historicalNote: The question asks how lasting promises fit a broken crown and unanswered distress. The heading names Ethan the Ezrahite.

contextNote.title: A promise becomes grounds for protest
contextNote.text: For thirty-seven verses the poet praises a sworn promise. Verse 38 begins, “But you have rejected.” He quotes God’s oath and sets the facts beside it (verses 34–35, 39–45). Verse 49 asks where the sworn kindness has gone. He complains because he believes the promise. The poem gives no answer. A blessing in verse 52 closes the third part of the Psalms.

chapters.title: Teach us to number our days
chapters.summary: The heading calls this a prayer of Moses. The Lord has been his people’s home in every generation. He was God before the mountains were born. A thousand years are like a day to him. People are like grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening. A life lasts seventy or eighty years and is full of toil. The speaker asks God to teach them to count their days. He asks God to establish the work of their hands.
chapters.meaning: Verses 3–10 set human life against God’s time. Verse 12 asks to be taught from that contrast. Counting days means knowing they are few. The hoped result is a wise heart. Verses 13–17 then ask for joy to match the years of trouble. The last verse asks twice that their work may last. This poem follows Psalm 89 and looks back before David to God as home.

lds.text: What does numbering days change about the purpose of work?

chapters.historicalNote: Awareness of limited time leads to a request for wisdom and useful work.

contextNote.title: Counting days leads to a request for lasting work
contextNote.text: Verses 3–10 set human life against God’s time. Verse 12 asks to be taught from that contrast. Counting days means knowing they are few. The hoped result is a wise heart. Verses 13–17 then ask for joy to match the years of trouble. The last verse asks twice that their work may last. This poem follows Psalm 89 and looks back before David to God as home.

chapters.title: Shelter under God’s wings
chapters.summary: The poem speaks of one who lives in the shelter of the Most High. God will save him from the hunter’s trap and from deadly disease. He covers him with his feathers. He need not fear terror by night or arrows by day. Angels will guard him and lift him up. Then God speaks. He will rescue the one who loves him and answer when he calls. He will be with him in trouble and give him long life.
chapters.meaning: Three voices speak in this poem. One says “I” in verse 2, and another addresses “you” in verses 3–13. God speaks as “I” in verses 14–16. Verse 15 is his promise. He will be “with him in trouble,” which assumes trouble comes. The devil quotes verses 11–12 to Jesus in Matthew 4:6. Jesus refuses to use the promise to test God.

lds.text: Which images make the promise of shelter vivid?

chapters.historicalNote: Its images express confident trust. They belong to a song rather than a prediction for every life.

contextNote.title: Protection is spoken through changing voices
contextNote.text: Three voices speak in this poem. One says “I” in verse 2, and another addresses “you” in verses 3–13. God speaks as “I” in verses 14–16. Verse 15 is his promise. He will be “with him in trouble,” which assumes trouble comes. The devil quotes verses 11–12 to Jesus in Matthew 4:6. Jesus refuses to use the promise to test God.

chapters.title: A Sabbath song of lasting growth
chapters.summary: The heading calls this a song for the Sabbath day. It is good to thank the LORD with harp and lyre. His works make the speaker glad, and his thoughts are deep. A senseless person does not understand this. The wicked sprout like grass and are destroyed forever. The righteous flourish like a palm and grow like a cedar. They are planted in the LORD’s house. They still bear fruit in old age.
chapters.meaning: The poem compares two kinds of growth. Verse 7 says the wicked spring up like grass, which does not last. Verse 12 gives the righteous the palm and the cedar. Those trees grow slowly and stand for generations. Verse 14 says they stay green and fruitful in old age. Verse 3 names the lyre among the instruments of this praise. The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison only.

lds.text: What kind of growth remains possible in old age?

chapters.historicalNote: Trees near God’s house picture a life that keeps bearing fruit beyond youth.

contextNote.title: Two kinds of growth have different futures

Those trees grow slowly and stand for generations. Verse 14 says they stay green and fruitful in old age. Verse 3 names the lyre among the instruments of this praise. chapters.title: The king above the flood
chapters.summary: The LORD reigns and is robed in majesty. He has made the world firm, and it cannot be moved. His throne was set up long ago. The floods have lifted up their voice and their pounding waves. The LORD on high is mightier than the thunder of many waters. His decrees are very sure. Holiness belongs to his house forever.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 says “lifted up” three times, like water rising. The sea stands for forces no person can control. Verse 4 does not describe a fight. The LORD is simply “on high,” above the breakers. Verse 2 says his throne was in place before the floods rose. Verse 5 turns from the sea to God’s decrees. His firmness is found in teaching that can be trusted.

lds.text: How does the flood help explain enduring rule?

chapters.historicalNote: The threatening flood gives scale to a greater stability in God’s reign.

contextNote.title: Rising waters meet an established throne

The LORD is simply “on high,” above the breakers. Verse 2 says his throne was in place before the floods rose. Verse 5 turns from the sea to God’s decrees. chapters.title: Justice for people harmed by rulers
chapters.summary: The speaker calls on God to rise as judge of the earth. The wicked crush God’s people. They kill the widow, the foreigner, and the orphan. They say the LORD does not see. The speaker answers that the maker of the ear can hear. The LORD will not abandon his people. When the speaker’s foot slipped, God’s kindness held him up. He asks whether a wicked throne that makes harm legal can be God’s ally.
chapters.meaning: Verses 5–6 name the victims: widows, foreigners, and orphans. Exodus 22:21–22 protected exactly those groups. Verse 7 gives the rulers’ theory that God does not see. Verse 9 answers that the one who made the eye can see. Verse 20 names the worst form of harm. It is done “by statute,” through the law itself. The verse asks whether such a court can claim God’s support.

lds.text: Why must unjust laws receive the same examination as unjust actions?

chapters.historicalNote: The poem names harmful laws as well as harmful acts. Legal power does not make injustice right.

contextNote.title: The prayer names harm made legal
contextNote.text: Verses 5–6 name the victims: widows, foreigners, and orphans. Exodus 22:21–22 protected exactly those groups. Verse 7 gives the rulers’ theory that God does not see. chapters.title: Praise without a hardened heart
chapters.summary: The poem invites the people to sing to the LORD, their rock. He is a great King above all gods. The depths, the mountains, and the sea are his. They are called to kneel before their Maker. They are the sheep of his hand. Then a warning comes: hear his voice today. Do not harden your hearts as at Meribah in the wilderness. That generation tested God and did not enter his rest.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–7 are a glad call to worship. In the middle of verse 7 the tone changes. God’s own voice warns the kneeling people. Verse 8 recalls Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:1–7). Those people had seen God’s works and still tested him. “Today” makes each hearing of God’s voice a new test. The poem ends on the warning and does not soften it.

lds.text: What must worshipers learn from the wilderness warning?

chapters.historicalNote: Worship must include listening. Earlier refusal becomes a warning for the present gathering.

contextNote.title: An invitation changes into a warning
contextNote.text: Verses 1–7 are a glad call to worship. In the middle of verse 7 the tone changes. God’s own voice warns the kneeling people. Verse 8 recalls Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:1–7). chapters.title: Tell the nations about the Lord
chapters.summary: The poem calls all the earth to sing a new song to the LORD. His glory should be told among the nations. The gods of the peoples are idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Families of nations should bring him an offering. They should say that the LORD reigns and judges fairly. The heavens, the earth, and the sea are called to rejoice. The fields and the trees of the forest sing. He is coming to judge the earth with justice.
chapters.meaning: The circle of singers widens through the poem. It begins with the earth’s peoples (verses 1 and 7). Verses 11–12 add the sky, the sea, the fields, and the trees. Verse 13 gives the reason for their joy. The LORD is coming to judge. Judgment here means setting things right. A world harmed by wrong has reason to sing about that.

lds.text: Why does the earth rejoice at the promise of fair judgment?

chapters.historicalNote: The coming judgment is cause for joy because it promises fairness for the world.

contextNote.title: Creation joins the nations’ song
contextNote.text: The circle of singers widens through the poem. It begins with the earth’s peoples (verses 1 and 7). Verses 11–12 add the sky, the sea, the fields, and the trees. Verse 13 gives the reason for their joy. The LORD is coming to judge. Judgment here means setting things right. A world harmed by wrong has reason to sing about that.

chapters.title: Light for those who love justice
chapters.summary: The LORD reigns, and the earth should be glad. Clouds and darkness surround him. Justice is the base of his throne. Fire goes before him, and the mountains melt like wax. The heavens declare his justice. All who worship idols are put to shame. Those who love the LORD must hate evil. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the honest in heart.
chapters.meaning: Verses 2–6 describe fire, lightning, and melting mountains. After that display the poem gives one command. Verse 10 says those who love the LORD must hate evil. Love for God is defined by what a person refuses. The same verse promises that he guards their lives. Verse 11 says light is “sown,” like seed that grows later. The presence that burns enemies in verse 3 gives light to the righteous.

lds.text: What choices should follow the call to love justice?

chapters.historicalNote: The call to hate evil turns praise into a choice about conduct.

contextNote.title: Cosmic power leads to a demand about conduct
contextNote.text: Verses 2–6 describe fire, lightning, and melting mountains. After that display the poem gives one command. Verse 10 says those who love the LORD must hate evil. Love for God is defined by what a person refuses. The same verse promises that he guards their lives. Verse 11 says light is “sown,” like seed that grows later. The presence that burns enemies in verse 3 gives light to the righteous.

chapters.title: A new song for rescue
chapters.summary: The poem calls for a new song, since the LORD has done wonderful things. His right hand has won the victory. He has shown his saving power to the nations. He remembered his kindness to Israel. All the earth should shout with lyre, trumpets, and horn. The sea should roar, and the rivers clap their hands. The mountains should sing together. The LORD is coming to judge the world fairly.
chapters.meaning: Three choirs sing in this poem. People play the lyre and trumpets (verses 4–6). The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison for such strings. The sea and its creatures roar (verse 7). Rivers clap and mountains sing (verse 8). Verse 9 gives one reason: the LORD comes to judge with fairness. People who have been wronged can hear that as good news.

lds.text: How does the praise expand beyond the people who first received rescue?

chapters.historicalNote: The widening celebration connects Israel’s rescue with fair judgment for the whole earth.

contextNote.title: Judgment becomes a reason for music
contextNote.text: Three choirs sing in this poem. People play the lyre and trumpets (verses 4–6). The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison for such strings. The sea and its creatures roar (verse 7). Rivers clap and mountains sing (verse 8). Verse 9 gives one reason: the LORD comes to judge with fairness. People who have been wronged can hear that as good news.

chapters.title: A holy ruler who answers
chapters.summary: The LORD reigns, and the peoples tremble. He sits enthroned above the cherubim. He is holy. The King loves justice and has established fairness in Israel. Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called on him, and he answered. He spoke to them from the pillar of cloud. He forgave them, and he also punished their wrongs. The people are called to worship at his holy hill.
chapters.meaning: “Holy” closes each part of the poem (verses 3, 5, 9). Verse 8 shows what that holiness looks like in practice. God answered his servants and forgave them. He also held them to account for what they did. Moses and Aaron are themselves examples. They were forgiven, and they still did not enter the land (Numbers 20:12). The verse keeps mercy and justice together.

lds.text: How do forgiveness and correction appear together in the remembered answers?

chapters.historicalNote: Answered prayer includes both forgiveness and correction. Holiness does not remove accountability.

contextNote.title: Forgiveness and accountability stand together
contextNote.text: “Holy” closes each part of the poem (verses 3, 5, 9). Verse 8 shows what that holiness looks like in practice. God answered his servants and forgave them. chapters.title: Enter with thanks
chapters.summary: This short psalm of thanks calls all lands to shout to the LORD. They should serve him with gladness and come with singing. They should know that the LORD is God. He made them, and they are his. They are his people and the sheep of his pasture. They should enter his gates with thanks and his courts with praise. The LORD is good. His kindness lasts forever, and his faithfulness reaches every generation.
chapters.meaning: The psalm gives seven commands, and “know” stands in the middle. Verse 3 says what there is to know. The LORD made us, so we belong to him. That belonging comes before the call to enter in verse 4. The invitation in verse 1 goes to “all you lands.” Verse 5 gives three reasons for the thanks. The LORD is good, kind, and faithful.

lds.text: What does belonging contribute to the people’s gratitude?

chapters.historicalNote: The short invitation grounds gratitude in belonging and care across generations.

contextNote.title: Belonging leads into the invitation to enter
contextNote.text: The psalm gives seven commands, and “know” stands in the middle. Verse 3 says what there is to know. The LORD made us, so we belong to him. That belonging comes before the call to enter in verse 4. The invitation in verse 1 goes to “all you lands.” Verse 5 gives three reasons for the thanks. The LORD is good, kind, and faithful.

chapters.title: A ruler’s promises for his household
chapters.summary: A ruler sings of kindness and justice. He promises to live with a blameless heart inside his own house. He will set nothing worthless before his eyes. He will silence anyone who slanders a neighbor in secret. He will not put up with proud looks. He will look for faithful people to live with him and serve him. No liar will stay in his house. Each morning he will remove the wicked from the LORD’s city.
chapters.meaning: The ruler’s pledge begins at home (verse 2). It then turns to the people he keeps near him. The poem uses “eyes” in two ways. Verse 3 says what he will not look at. Verse 6 says whom he will look for: the faithful of the land. He chooses his servants by their conduct. Verse 8 shows the result reaching the whole city.

lds.text: Which household choices could support or undermine a ruler’s public promises?

chapters.historicalNote: Fair rule begins with the choices made close to home, not only public promises.

contextNote.title: A household becomes a model of public rule
contextNote.text: The ruler’s pledge begins at home (verse 2). It then turns to the people he keeps near him. The poem uses “eyes” in two ways. Verse 3 says what he will not look at. Verse 6 says whom he will look for: the faithful of the land. He chooses his servants by their conduct. Verse 8 shows the result reaching the whole city.

chapters.title: An afflicted person waits for Zion’s renewal
chapters.summary: The heading calls this the prayer of a suffering person who is faint. His days vanish like smoke, and his heart is withered like grass. He is like a lonely bird on a roof. His enemies mock him, and he eats ashes with his bread. Yet the LORD sits enthroned forever. He will rise and have mercy on Zion. This will be written for a generation still to come. The heavens will wear out like clothing, but God stays the same.
chapters.meaning: The speaker’s days are short (verses 3, 11, 23). God’s years have no end (verses 12 and 24–27). Verse 18 builds a bridge between the two. His prayer will be written for people not yet created. His words will outlast him even if he does not recover. The poem joins one man’s illness with a ruined city (verses 13–16). Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes verses 25–27.

lds.text: Why does the speaker look toward generations beyond his own brief life?

chapters.historicalNote: A brief human life is set beside God’s endurance and hope for later generations.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: A failing life seeks an enduring record
contextNote.text: The speaker’s days are short (verses 3, 11, 23). God’s years have no end (verses 12 and 24–27). Verse 18 builds a bridge between the two. His prayer will be written for people not yet created. His words will outlast him even if he does not recover. The poem joins one man’s illness with a ruined city (verses 13–16). Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes verses 25–27.

chapters.title: Remember mercy and human frailty
chapters.summary: The speaker tells his soul to bless the LORD and forget none of his gifts. God forgives, heals, and rescues his life from the pit. He is merciful and gracious and slow to anger. He does not treat people as their sins deserve. His kindness is as high as the heavens are above the earth. He pities his children as a father does. He remembers that people are dust. Human life is like grass, but his kindness lasts forever.
chapters.meaning: Verse 13 compares God to a father who pities his children. Verse 14 gives the reason with the word “For.” He knows how humans are formed, and he remembers the dust (Genesis 2:7). A maker’s knowledge leads here to compassion, not contempt. Verses 11–12 measure that mercy by height and by distance. Verses 15–17 set short human life beside lasting kindness. Verse 8 quotes God’s own words about himself from Exodus 34:6.

lds.text: How does remembering human weakness support compassion?

chapters.historicalNote: Awareness of weakness supports compassion rather than contempt for those who fail.

contextNote.title: Mercy takes human limits into account
contextNote.text: Verse 13 compares God to a father who pities his children. Verse 14 gives the reason with the word “For.” He knows how humans are formed, and he remembers the dust (Genesis 2:7). A maker’s knowledge leads here to compassion, not contempt. Verses 11–12 measure that mercy by height and by distance. Verses 15–17 set short human life beside lasting kindness. Verse 8 quotes God’s own words about himself from Exodus 34:6.

chapters.title: A world supplied with life
chapters.summary: The speaker blesses the LORD, who is clothed with light. God stretched out the heavens and set the earth on its foundations. He sends springs into the valleys for the wild animals. He grows grass for cattle and plants, wine, oil, and bread for people. Lions hunt at night, and people work by day. The sea holds creatures beyond number. All of them wait for God to give their food. He takes their breath, and they die; he sends his Spirit, and they are created.
chapters.meaning: “These all” in verse 27 covers sea creatures, lions, cattle, and people. Humans are one entry in the list (verses 14–15 and 23). Lions take the night, and people take the day (verses 20–23). They share one world on different shifts. Verse 28 pictures God’s open hand. Verses 29–30 say every breath depends on him. Leviathan appears in verse 26 as a creature at play.

lds.text: How do water, plants, animals, and people depend on one another in this poem?

chapters.historicalNote: Many kinds of life depend on provision beyond their own strength.

contextNote.title: Creation includes many dependent lives
contextNote.text: “These all” in verse 27 covers sea creatures, lions, cattle, and people. Humans are one entry in the list (verses 14–15 and 23). Lions take the night, and people take the day (verses 20–23). They share one world on different shifts. Verse 28 pictures God’s open hand. Verses 29–30 say every breath depends on him. Leviathan appears in verse 26 as a creature at play.

chapters.title: Remember the promise and the journey
chapters.summary: The poem calls the people to remember the LORD’s wonders. He made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and promised them a land. When they were few, he protected them. He sent Joseph ahead as a slave, and Joseph rose to rule Egypt. Israel grew there and was hated. God sent Moses, Aaron, and the plagues. He brought his people out with joy and fed them in the desert. He gave them lands so that they would keep his laws.
chapters.meaning: Genesis 37 says Joseph’s brothers sold him. Verse 17 names another subject: “He sent a man before them.” The poem reads that sale from the end of the story. Verse 18 does not hide the irons on his neck. Verse 19 says the waiting tested him. Joseph gives this reading himself in Genesis 45:5–8. This poem tells only God’s faithful acts, and Psalm 106 tells the other side.

lds.text: What responsibility follows the remembered gift of land?

chapters.historicalNote: The long memory connects the gift of land with a call to keep God’s teaching.

contextNote.title: A remembered story changes the meaning of hardship

chapters.title: Confession through the people’s history
chapters.summary: The poem begins with praise and a prayer to be remembered. Then it confesses: we have sinned as our fathers did. The fathers forgot God’s wonders at the Red Sea. They craved food in the desert and envied Moses. They made a calf at Horeb, and Moses stood in the gap for them. They joined in the worship of Baal and later sacrificed their children. God gave them over to the nations many times. Yet he heard their cry and remembered his covenant.
chapters.meaning: Psalm 105 told this history as God’s faithfulness. This poem tells it as Israel’s failure. Verse 6 puts the singers inside the story: “We have sinned with our fathers.” They do not say “they sinned.” Each rebellion in the poem is met by mercy (verses 8, 23, 44–45). Verse 47 shows why they sing it. They are scattered and ask to be gathered.

lds.text: Why does confession include harms done in earlier generations?

chapters.historicalNote: Remembering wrongdoing becomes part of asking for rescue. The account includes harm to children.

contextNote.title: A historical song includes its present singers
contextNote.text: Psalm 105 told this history as God’s faithfulness. This poem tells it as Israel’s failure. Verse 47 shows why they sing it. They are scattered and ask to be gathered.

chapters.title: Give thanks after different kinds of danger
chapters.summary: The poem calls the redeemed to thank the LORD. It describes four groups in trouble. Some wandered hungry in the desert. Some sat in dark prisons because they had rebelled. Some were sick through their own folly. Some were caught in a storm at sea. Each group cried to the LORD, and he rescued them. He turns rivers into desert and desert into pools, and the wise will consider this.
chapters.meaning: Two lines repeat for each group. They cried, and he delivered them (verses 6, 13, 19, 28). Then comes the call to give thanks (verses 8, 15, 21, 31). The travelers and sailors did nothing wrong. The prisoners and the sick brought trouble on themselves (verses 11 and 17). God answers the cry in all four cases. Verse 31 speaks of his deeds for “the children of men.”

lds.text: What do the four different rescues have in common?

chapters.historicalNote: Different situations share a repeated call to recognize kindness after help arrives.

contextNote.title: Repeated rescues invite different groups to answer
contextNote.text: Two lines repeat for each group. They cried, and he delivered them (verses 6, 13, 19, 28). Then comes the call to give thanks (verses 8, 15, 21, 31). The travelers and sailors did nothing wrong. The prisoners and the sick brought trouble on themselves (verses 11 and 17). God answers the cry in all four cases. Verse 31 speaks of his deeds for “the children of men.”

chapters.title: Praise followed by a plea for victory
chapters.summary: The speaker’s heart is steady, and he will sing and wake the dawn. He will give thanks among the nations. God’s kindness is higher than the heavens. He asks God to save with his right hand. God has spoken: Shechem, Gilead, Ephraim, and Judah are his. Moab, Edom, and Philistia are under him. Yet God has not gone out with their armies. With God they will still do bravely.
chapters.meaning: This poem joins parts of two older ones (57:7–11 and 60:5–12). It leaves out the laments that opened both. Old words are used again for a new need. Verse 7 repeats God’s claim to each region. Verse 11 still admits that he has not marched with the army. The promise is held up while the victory is awaited. The steady heart of verse 1 comes before any change.

lds.text: What does the speaker ask for after beginning with praise?

chapters.historicalNote: The images of land concern rule and conflict. They do not describe a new journey.

contextNote.title: A steadfast singer still awaits victory

chapters.title: Anger against an accuser
chapters.summary: The speaker asks God not to stay silent. Liars surround him and attack him without cause. They repay his love with accusation, and he prays. A long series of curses follows. The accused man should lose his office, his family, and his name. He never showed kindness and hunted the poor to death. The speaker is poor, weak from fasting, and mocked. He asks God to save him, for God stands beside the needy.
chapters.meaning: Verse 4 gives the speaker’s answer to betrayal: he prays. He brings the matter to God as a case. The curses in verses 6–19 are the longest in the Psalms. Some readers take them as his accusers’ words quoted back. The text does not mark them either way. Verse 16 states the charge: this man hunted the poor. Verse 31 sets the LORD at the right hand of the needy.

lds.text: How far does the speaker’s anger extend beyond the accused enemy?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer records intense anger. Its wishes extend harm to the enemy’s family.

contextNote.title: The complaint turns failed love into a public case

Some readers take them as his accusers’ words quoted back. The text does not mark them either way. Verse 16 states the charge: this man hunted the poor. chapters.title: A royal figure and a priest
chapters.summary: The LORD tells the speaker’s lord to sit at his right hand. His enemies will become his footstool. The LORD will extend his rule from Zion. His people offer themselves freely on the day of battle. The LORD has sworn an oath and will not change it. This ruler is a priest forever, like Melchizedek. The Lord at his right hand will shatter kings. He will judge the nations and lift up his head.
chapters.meaning: The poem contains two sayings from God. Verse 1 gives a throne, and verse 4 gives a priesthood by oath. In Israel kings came from Judah and priests from Levi. King Uzziah was punished for acting as a priest (2 Chronicles 26:18). Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18 was both king and priest before Levi lived. Verse 4 gives the ruler that older kind of office. Hebrews 5–7 applies it to Jesus Christ.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the king and priest with Jesus Christ. What duties do these roles carry?

chapters.historicalNote: Royal and priestly images stand together. Later readers apply them to the Messiah.

contextNote.title: Royal authority joins another office
contextNote.text: The poem contains two sayings from God. Verse 1 gives a throne, and verse 4 gives a priesthood by oath. In Israel kings came from Judah and priests from Levi. King Uzziah was punished for acting as a priest (2 Chronicles 26:18). Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18 was both king and priest before Levi lived. Verse 4 gives the ruler that older kind of office. Hebrews 5–7 applies it to Jesus Christ.

chapters.title: Remember the works of the Lord
chapters.summary: The speaker will thank the LORD with his whole heart among the upright. The LORD’s works are great and are studied by all who enjoy them. He is gracious and merciful. He gives food to those who fear him and remembers his covenant. He gave his people the lands of other nations. His commands are trustworthy and lasting. He sent redemption to his people. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
chapters.meaning: Each line of this poem begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Verse 2 says God’s works are to be studied. Verse 4 says they are to be remembered. Verse 5 gives two examples: food and a covenant kept. The poem then moves from works to commands (verse 7). Remembering what God did leads to trusting what he says. Verse 10 calls that the start of wisdom.

lds.text: How should remembering God’s gifts affect what people do?

chapters.historicalNote: Remembered help leads toward wisdom expressed in keeping God’s commands.

contextNote.title: Remembered works lead toward practiced wisdom

chapters.title: Generosity in a secure household
chapters.summary: The poem blesses the person who fears the LORD and delights in his commands. His children will be strong, and his house will have wealth. Light rises in the dark for the upright. He is gracious, lends freely, and runs his affairs justly. He will not be shaken or fear bad news. His heart is steady. He gives freely to the poor. The wicked see it, are angry, and melt away.
chapters.meaning: This poem pairs with Psalm 111 and uses the same alphabet form. Psalm 111 called God gracious and merciful (111:4). Verse 4 here uses those words for the person who fears him. The worshiper comes to resemble the one he worships. His wealth in verse 3 does not stay in his house. He lends in verse 5 and scatters gifts to the poor in verse 9. Second Corinthians 9:9 quotes verse 9.

lds.text: How does generosity enter the poem’s picture of strength?

chapters.historicalNote: Its picture of strength includes generosity. Security does not require withholding help from neighbors.

contextNote.title: A blessed life includes giving away
contextNote.text: This poem pairs with Psalm 111 and uses the same alphabet form. Psalm 111 called God gracious and merciful (111:4). Verse 4 here uses those words for the person who fears him. chapters.title: The high God lifts the lowly
chapters.summary: The poem calls the LORD’s servants to praise his name. His name is to be praised from sunrise to sunset. The LORD is high above all nations. No one is like him, seated on high. He stoops to look at the heavens and the earth. He raises the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap. He seats them with princes. He gives the childless woman a home and makes her a joyful mother.
chapters.meaning: Verses 4–5 place the LORD above the nations and above the sky. Verse 6 says he must stoop even to see the heavens. From that height he attends to the lowest places. Verse 7 names the dust and the ash heap. Verse 8 seats those people among princes. Verse 9 adds a woman without children. Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2:8 uses nearly the same words.

lds.text: What does lifting poor people reveal about greatness?

chapters.historicalNote: Greatness appears through attention to people others overlook.

contextNote.title: Great height is expressed through attention below
contextNote.text: Verses 4–5 place the LORD above the nations and above the sky. Verse 6 says he must stoop even to see the heavens. From that height he attends to the lowest places. Verse 7 names the dust and the ash heap. Verse 8 seats those people among princes. Verse 9 adds a woman without children. Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2:8 uses nearly the same words.

chapters.title: The earth responds to the departure from Egypt
chapters.summary: Israel went out of Egypt, from a people of foreign speech. Judah became God’s sanctuary. The sea saw it and fled, and the Jordan turned back. The mountains skipped like rams and the hills like lambs. The poet asks the sea and the river why they ran. He asks the mountains why they skipped. The earth should tremble before the God of Jacob. He turned the rock into a pool of water.
chapters.meaning: The poem joins two crossings into one event. The sea parts at the exodus, and the Jordan parts at the entry. In verses 5–6 the poet teases the sea, river, and hills with questions. He does not name God until verse 7. Verse 2 says only “his” sanctuary. The delay builds suspense toward the answer. Verse 8 ends with rock turned to water, the reverse of sea turned to land.

lds.text: How do the landscape images give form to the people’s rescue?

chapters.historicalNote: The landscape becomes a poetic witness to the people’s rescue and God’s provision of water.

contextNote.title: Questions make the landscape a participant
contextNote.text: The poem joins two crossings into one event. The sea parts at the exodus, and the Jordan parts at the entry. In verses 5–6 the poet teases the sea, river, and hills with questions. He does not name God until verse 7. Verse 2 says only “his” sanctuary. The delay builds suspense toward the answer. Verse 8 ends with rock turned to water, the reverse of sea turned to land.

chapters.title: Living trust and lifeless idols
chapters.summary: The people ask that glory go to the LORD’s name and not to them. The nations ask where their God is. He is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases. The nations’ idols are silver and gold, made by human hands. They have mouths, eyes, ears, and hands that do nothing. Those who make them will become like them. Israel should trust the LORD, their help and shield. He will bless those who fear him, small and great.
chapters.meaning: Verses 5–7 go through the idol’s body part by part. Mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, and throat all fail. Verse 8 states the cost to the worshiper. People become like what they trust. They grow unable to see, hear, or speak truly. Verse 3 describes the opposite kind of God. He cannot be seen, and he acts.

lds.text: What does the contrast with idols suggest about the effects of trust?

chapters.historicalNote: The idols have body parts but cannot act. Trust shapes what worshipers become like.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: Made objects reveal the limits of their makers’ trust
contextNote.text: Verses 5–7 go through the idol’s body part by part. Mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, and throat all fail. Verse 8 states the cost to the worshiper. People become like what they trust. They grow unable to see, hear, or speak truly. Verse 3 describes the opposite kind of God. He cannot be seen, and he acts.

chapters.title: Thanks after a plea near death
chapters.summary: The speaker loves the LORD, who heard his cry. The cords of death had wrapped around him. He called on the LORD’s name and was saved. God rescued his life from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from falling. He asks what he can give back to the LORD. He will lift the cup of salvation and call on the LORD’s name. He will keep his vows before all the people. He will offer thanks in the courts of the LORD’s house.
chapters.meaning: Verse 12 asks what a rescued person can give in return. The answer in verse 13 is surprising. He will take a cup, so he receives again. He will also keep calling on the LORD’s name. Verse 14 adds vows kept in public. Gratitude is shown by continued dependence and open thanks. Verse 15 says the death of God’s faithful ones is costly to him.

lds.text: Why does the speaker promise thanks before other people?

chapters.historicalNote: Rescue leads to gratitude expressed before others, not only private relief.

contextNote.title: Gratitude asks what response can be given
contextNote.text: Verse 12 asks what a rescued person can give in return. The answer in verse 13 is surprising. He will take a cup, so he receives again. He will also keep calling on the LORD’s name. Verse 14 adds vows kept in public. Gratitude is shown by continued dependence and open thanks. Verse 15 says the death of God’s faithful ones is costly to him.

chapters.title: Every nation is called to praise
chapters.summary: This is the shortest psalm. It calls all nations to praise the LORD. It calls all peoples to honor him. The reason is that his kindness toward us is great. His faithfulness lasts forever.
chapters.meaning: The poem has two verses and the widest audience. Verse 1 speaks to every nation and people. Verse 2 gives the reason, and it is Israel’s own experience. God’s kindness has been great “toward us.” What he did for one people is offered as cause for all to praise. Romans 15:11 quotes verse 1 about the nations joining in.

lds.text: How does the brief invitation reach beyond one nation?

chapters.historicalNote: Its two verses widen the invitation beyond Israel while keeping the reason for praise clear.

contextNote.title: A very short song has a wide audience
contextNote.text: The poem has two verses and the widest audience. Verse 1 speaks to every nation and people. Verse 2 gives the reason, and it is Israel’s own experience. God’s kindness has been great “toward us.” What he did for one people is offered as cause for all to praise. Romans 15:11 quotes verse 1 about the nations joining in.

chapters.title: The rejected stone becomes central
chapters.summary: The people give thanks, for the LORD’s kindness lasts forever. The speaker called in distress, and the LORD set him free. Nations surrounded him like bees, and he cut them off in the LORD’s name. He was pushed hard and nearly fell. He will not die but live and tell what the LORD has done. He asks for the gates to be opened. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The people bless the one who comes in the LORD’s name.
chapters.meaning: Builders are the experts, and they judged this stone unfit. Verse 22 says it now holds the chief place. Verse 23 credits the change to the LORD alone. In the poem the stone is the speaker himself. He was near death and now enters the gates (verses 17–20). Jesus quotes verse 22 in Matthew 21:42. The crowd in Matthew 21:9 shouts words from verses 25–26.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the rejected stone with Jesus Christ. How does the stone’s place change?

chapters.historicalNote: Rejection does not settle the stone’s worth. Deliverance changes its place in the community.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: Rejected value returns in a building image
contextNote.text: Builders are the experts, and they judged this stone unfit. Verse 22 says it now holds the chief place. Verse 23 credits the change to the LORD alone. In the poem the stone is the speaker himself. He was near death and now enters the gates (verses 17–20). Jesus quotes verse 22 in Matthew 21:42. The crowd in Matthew 21:9 shouts words from verses 25–26.

chapters.title: Learning God’s teaching through a long prayer
chapters.summary: This is the longest psalm. It has twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Almost every verse names God’s teaching as law, word, statute, or command. The speaker is young and feels like a stranger on the earth. Princes slander him, and he has suffered. He says God’s word is a lamp for his feet. He loves the commands more than gold. He ends by saying he has strayed like a lost sheep.
chapters.meaning: For one hundred seventy-five verses the speaker declares his love for God’s teaching. The last verse is a confession. He has gone astray like a lost sheep. He asks God to seek him. Earlier he said he sought God with his whole heart (verses 2 and 10). Now the seeker needs to be found. Long devotion has not removed his need for rescue, and he still remembers the commands.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson explains the Hebrew alphabet sections. Come, Follow Me studies scripture as guidance. What help does the speaker request while facing hardship?

chapters.historicalNote: Its 22 sections follow Hebrew alphabet letters. Each section has eight verses about God’s teaching.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: Devotion leaves room for being lost
contextNote.text: For one hundred seventy-five verses the speaker declares his love for God’s teaching. The last verse is a confession. He has gone astray like a lost sheep. He asks God to seek him. Earlier he said he sought God with his whole heart (verses 2 and 10). Now the seeker needs to be found. Long devotion has not removed his need for rescue, and he still remembers the commands.

chapters.title: Peace among people who seek war
chapters.summary: This is the first of fifteen songs of ascents. The speaker cried to the LORD in distress and was answered. He asks to be saved from lying lips. He asks what a deceitful tongue deserves: sharp arrows and burning coals. He grieves that he lives in Meshech and among the tents of Kedar. He has lived too long with people who hate peace. He is for peace. When he speaks, they are for war.
chapters.meaning: Psalms 120–134 carry the heading “A Song of Ascents.” The first one begins far from home. Genesis 10:2 and 25:13 list Meshech and Kedar among other nations. He lives among people who are hostile to him. Verse 7 gives the whole conflict in one line. He speaks for peace, and they answer with war. The journey of these songs starts from not belonging.

lds.text: What does the speaker seek while surrounded by people who want war?

chapters.historicalNote: Meshech and Kedar express distance and hostility. The poem does not give a travel sequence.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: Speech begins the songs of ascent amid conflict
contextNote.text: Psalms 120–134 carry the heading “A Song of Ascents.” The first one begins far from home. Genesis 10:2 and 25:13 list Meshech and Kedar among other nations. He lives among people who are hostile to him. Verse 7 gives the whole conflict in one line. He speaks for peace, and they answer with war. The journey of these songs starts from not belonging.

chapters.title: Help from the maker of heaven and earth
chapters.summary: The speaker lifts his eyes to the hills and asks where his help comes from. It comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth. God will not let his foot slip. The one who keeps Israel does not slumber or sleep. The LORD is his keeper and his shade. The sun will not harm him by day or the moon by night. The LORD will keep him from all evil. He will guard his going out and coming in forever.
chapters.meaning: The words “keep” and “keeper” appear six times in eight verses. The voice changes after verse 2. “I” asks the question, and then someone answers with “you.” Verse 3 names two dangers of a journey. A foot may slip, and a guard may fall asleep. Verse 4 says this guard never does. The remaining verses cover day, night, departure, and return.

lds.text: How does the keeper’s wakefulness answer the traveler’s need?

chapters.historicalNote: The keeper’s wakefulness answers the traveler’s need for protection along the way.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: The keeper’s wakefulness answers human vulnerability
contextNote.text: The words “keep” and “keeper” appear six times in eight verses. The voice changes after verse 2. “I” asks the question, and then someone answers with “you.” Verse 3 names two dangers of a journey. A foot may slip, and a guard may fall asleep. chapters.title: Prayer for Jerusalem’s peace
chapters.summary: The speaker was glad when people said, “Let’s go to the LORD’s house.” Now his feet stand inside Jerusalem’s gates. The city is built firmly together. The tribes go up there to give thanks to the LORD. Thrones for judgment stand there, the thrones of David’s house. He calls for prayer for Jerusalem’s peace. He wishes peace within its walls. He seeks its good for the sake of his family and the LORD’s house.
chapters.meaning: The pilgrim arrives in verse 2. Verses 4–5 name what the city is for: worship and justice. Verse 6 then gives the arrival a duty. Those who come must pray for the city’s peace. Verses 8–9 give two reasons. He prays for the sake of his brothers and friends. He prays for the sake of God’s house, and not for his own gain.

lds.text: What would peace require for people inside Jerusalem’s walls?

chapters.historicalNote: Love for the city includes concern for the people who live and worship there.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: Arrival becomes a duty toward the city
contextNote.text: The pilgrim arrives in verse 2. Verses 4–5 name what the city is for: worship and justice. Verse 6 then gives the arrival a duty. Those who come must pray for the city’s peace. Verses 8–9 give two reasons. He prays for the sake of his brothers and friends. He prays for the sake of God’s house, and not for his own gain.

chapters.title: A plea from people treated with contempt
chapters.summary: The speaker lifts his eyes to the one enthroned in heaven. Servants watch the hand of their master. A maid watches the hand of her mistress. In the same way the people watch the LORD until he shows mercy. They ask for mercy twice. They have had more than enough contempt. They are worn out by the scorn of the comfortable and the proud.
chapters.meaning: Verse 2 compares the people to household servants. A servant watches the master’s hand for a signal or for provision. The verse names both men and women. The word “until” shows the gaze is kept up over time. The trouble in verses 3–4 is not violence. It is contempt from people who live at ease. The people look up to God while others look down on them.

lds.text: Why does contempt become the main burden in this prayer?

chapters.historicalNote: The image joins dependence with expectation. The prayer names contempt as a burden needing relief.

contextNote.title: Waiting is pictured through directed eyes
contextNote.text: Verse 2 compares the people to household servants. A servant watches the master’s hand for a signal or for provision. The verse names both men and women. The word “until” shows the gaze is kept up over time. The trouble in verses 3–4 is not violence. It is contempt from people who live at ease. The people look up to God while others look down on them.

chapters.title: What if the Lord had not helped?
chapters.summary: The people say what would have happened without the LORD on their side. When men attacked, they would have been swallowed alive. The flood would have swept over them. The raging waters would have gone over their heads. They bless the LORD, who did not give them to those teeth. They escaped like a bird from a hunter’s trap. The trap broke. Their help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–2 begin twice with “If it had not been the LORD.” The poem thanks God by imagining the other outcome. It pictures a beast that swallows (verse 3) and a flood (verses 4–5). Verse 6 pictures teeth that did not close. Verse 7 pictures a bird in a snare. The snare “is broken,” so the escape was not the bird’s skill. The size of the thanks matches what almost happened.

lds.text: What do the flood and trap images show about the danger the people escaped?

chapters.historicalNote: The imagined outcome makes rescue visible by describing what could have overwhelmed them.

chapters.title: Steadfast trust and crooked paths
chapters.summary: Those who trust the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved. Mountains surround Jerusalem. In the same way the LORD surrounds his people now and forever. Wicked rule will not stay over the land of the righteous. Otherwise the righteous might turn to doing wrong. The poet asks the LORD to do good to the good. Those who turn to crooked ways will be led away. Peace be on Israel.
chapters.meaning: Verse 2 draws on the land itself. Jerusalem sits among hills that stand around it. The LORD’s care is pictured as that ring. Verse 3 adds a realistic concern. If wicked rule lasted too long, even good people might give in. So the poem expects a limit on it for their sake. Its trust allows for human weakness.

lds.text: How does the surrounding mountain image describe steadfast trust?

chapters.historicalNote: The closing prayer asks for good treatment while warning against joining harmful conduct.

contextNote.title: A landscape surrounds a claim of care

chapters.title: Restoration and tears at planting
chapters.summary: When the LORD brought back Zion’s captives, the people were like dreamers. Their mouths were full of laughter and song. The nations said the LORD had done great things for them. The people agree and are glad. They ask the LORD to restore them again like streams in the Negev. Those who sow in tears will reap with joy. The one who goes out weeping with seed will return with sheaves.
chapters.meaning: Verses 1–3 remember a past rescue that felt like a dream. Verse 4 says “again,” so more is needed. The Negev is dry land in the south. Its stream beds lie empty and then fill suddenly with rain. Verses 5–6 give a slower picture: seed, waiting, and harvest. A hungry farmer plants grain he could have eaten. The poem asks for both kinds of renewal.

lds.text: Why does the harvest image begin with tears?

chapters.historicalNote: Planting with tears keeps hope connected to effort made before any harvest appears.

chapters.title: Work, rest, and children
chapters.summary: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders work for nothing. Unless the LORD guards the city, the guard stays awake for nothing. It is useless to rise early and stay up late in anxious toil. God gives sleep to those he loves. Children are a gift from the LORD. They are like arrows in a warrior’s hand. The man with many is blessed. They will stand with him against enemies at the gate.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 does not tell builders and guards to stop working. It says their work alone cannot secure the result. Verse 2 turns to long, anxious hours. Rising early and staying late adds nothing if God does not give. Sleep is named as his gift. “House” can also mean a family, and verses 3–5 turn to children. They too are received, not produced by effort.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies a home built with the Lord’s help. Why does the poem question anxious work?

chapters.historicalNote: The contrast challenges anxious labor that leaves no room for rest or trust. The heading names Solomon.

chapters.title: Blessing at the household table
chapters.summary: Everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways is blessed. He will eat what his own hands have worked for. His wife will be like a fruitful vine in his house. His children will be like olive shoots around his table. The poem asks the LORD to bless him from Zion. May he see Jerusalem’s good all his life. May he see his children’s children. Peace be on Israel.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 pictures a family meal with two plants. The vine and the olive were the land’s chief crops. Both take years to mature and then bear for a long time. The blessing is slow and lasting, like them. Verses 5–6 widen the view beyond the table. The household’s good is tied to Jerusalem’s good. The last line reaches to all Israel.

lds.text: How does a household’s good connect with peace in the wider community?

chapters.historicalNote: Household well-being connects with the wider community rather than remaining a private good.

chapters.title: A people remember repeated oppression
chapters.summary: Israel says it has been attacked many times since its youth. Yet its enemies have not won. Plowmen plowed its back and made their furrows long. The LORD is just and has cut the cords of the wicked. May all who hate Zion be turned back. May they be like grass on a roof that withers before it grows. No reaper fills his hands with it. No passerby gives it a blessing.
chapters.meaning: The whole nation speaks here as one person. Verse 3 pictures that person’s back as a plowed field. The furrows are the scars of whipping. “From my youth” reaches back to Egypt. Verse 2 states the result: they “have not prevailed.” Verse 4 says the LORD cut the cords, as one cuts a plow’s harness. Verses 6–8 compare the enemies to rooftop grass that yields no harvest.

lds.text: What does the image of plowing across people’s backs show about their suffering?

chapters.historicalNote: The image gives physical force to oppression. Survival does not make the earlier harm small.

contextNote.title: A wounded body represents a people’s history
contextNote.text: The whole nation speaks here as one person. Verse 3 pictures that person’s back as a plowed field. The furrows are the scars of whipping. “From my youth” reaches back to Egypt. Verse 2 states the result: they “have not prevailed.” Verse 4 says the LORD cut the cords, as one cuts a plow’s harness. Verses 6–8 compare the enemies to rooftop grass that yields no harvest.

chapters.title: Waiting from the depths
chapters.summary: The speaker cries to the LORD out of the depths. He asks the Lord to hear his voice. If God kept a record of sins, no one could stand. But with God there is forgiveness. The speaker waits for the LORD and hopes in his word. He waits more than watchmen wait for the morning. He tells Israel to hope in the LORD. With him is kindness and full redemption.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 shows that the “depths” include guilt. Verse 4 says forgiveness leads to reverence, not carelessness. Verse 6 compares the speaker to a night watchman. A watchman cannot hurry the dawn, and he knows it will come. The verse says the line twice, which makes the reader wait too. In verse 7 the single voice turns to the whole people. His own waiting becomes advice for Israel.

lds.text: Why does waiting for morning suit a prayer about forgiveness?

chapters.historicalNote: Hope rests in forgiveness rather than a claim to have avoided every wrong.

chapters.title: A quieted soul
chapters.summary: The speaker tells the LORD that his heart is not proud. His eyes are not raised too high. He does not busy himself with matters too great for him. He has calmed and quieted his soul. His soul is like a weaned child with its mother. He tells Israel to hope in the LORD now and forever.
chapters.meaning: This poem is three verses long. Verse 1 gives up the need to master things beyond him. Verse 2 describes the result with a child. A weaned child no longer cries for milk. It is content simply to be with its mother. The speaker says, “I have stilled” my soul, so the calm took effort. Verse 3 offers that calm hope to the whole people.

lds.text: What does the quieted child image suggest about ambition?

chapters.historicalNote: The child’s settled presence pictures trust without demands for greater status.

chapters.title: Remember David’s promise about worship
chapters.summary: The poem asks the LORD to remember David and his hardships. David swore not to rest until he found a place for the LORD. The people heard of the ark and went to worship at his footstool. They ask the LORD to arise and come to his resting place. The LORD swore that David’s sons would sit on his throne. The LORD has chosen Zion for his home. He will bless her food and satisfy her poor with bread. He will make David’s strength grow there.
chapters.meaning: Two oaths stand in this poem. David swears to find a home for the LORD (verses 2–5). The LORD swears to give David a lasting line (verses 11–12). Verse 13 adds a second choice: the LORD has chosen Zion. God’s answer goes beyond what was asked. Verse 9 asks for priests clothed in righteousness. Verse 16 promises salvation, and verse 15 adds bread for the poor.

lds.text: What obligations accompany the promise about David’s descendants?

chapters.historicalNote: Royal promise and worship belong together. The prayer also asks for faithful descendants and joyful priests.

contextNote.title: Two acts of choosing connect king and sanctuary

chapters.title: The goodness of living together
chapters.summary: The poem says how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity. It is like fine oil poured on the head. The oil runs down Aaron’s beard to the collar of his robes. It is like the dew of Mount Hermon falling on the hills of Zion. There the LORD commands his blessing. That blessing is life forever.
chapters.meaning: Both pictures in this poem move downward. Oil runs down from head to beard to robe (verse 2). Dew comes down from Hermon to Zion (verse 3). The oil is the priest’s anointing oil of Exodus 30:22–30. It is poured in plenty, not measured out. Hermon stands far north of Zion. So unity is pictured as a gift that arrives from above and beyond.

lds.text: How do oil and dew picture blessing shared with others?

chapters.historicalNote: The descending images picture a blessing shared rather than kept at its source.

contextNote.title: Unity is described as something spreading

chapters.title: Blessing in the night
chapters.summary: This is the last of the songs of ascents. It calls the LORD’s servants to bless him. They stand in the LORD’s house by night. They are told to lift their hands toward the holy place. Then a blessing is spoken in return. May the LORD, who made heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.
chapters.meaning: The poem moves in two directions. In verses 1–2 the servants bless the LORD. In verse 3 the LORD blesses “you.” It reads like an exchange of greetings. The servants named work at night, when no crowd is present. The blessing comes from Zion and from the maker of heaven and earth. The songs that began far away in Psalm 120 end inside God’s house.

lds.text: How do the two calls to bless connect worshipers with God?

chapters.historicalNote: The brief exchange joins the worshipers’ blessing of God with a blessing sent from Zion.

contextNote.title: Blessing travels in both directions
contextNote.text: The poem moves in two directions. In verses 1–2 the servants bless the LORD. In verse 3 the LORD blesses “you.” It reads like an exchange of greetings. The servants named work at night, when no crowd is present. The blessing comes from Zion and from the maker of heaven and earth. The songs that began far away in Psalm 120 end inside God’s house.

chapters.title: Praise above idols and earthly rulers
chapters.summary: The poem calls the LORD’s servants to praise his name. He chose Jacob for himself. He does whatever he pleases in heaven, earth, and sea. He brings clouds, lightning, and wind. He struck Egypt’s firstborn and defeated great kings. He gave their land to Israel. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by hands. Israel, Aaron’s house, and Levi’s house are called to bless the LORD.
chapters.meaning: This poem gathers lines from other texts, including Psalm 115:4–8. Its order makes the argument. Verses 5–12 describe a God who acts. He sends weather, strikes Egypt, and gives land. Verse 15 then describes the idols as metal shaped by hands. They have mouths and eyes and do nothing. Verse 14 adds that the LORD has compassion on his servants.

lds.text: Why does the poem remember rescue before describing lifeless idols?

chapters.historicalNote: The remembered acts contrast with idols that cannot speak, see, or hear.

contextNote.title: Memory supplies a contrast with lifeless images

chapters.title: Kindness remembered in every line
chapters.summary: The poem calls the people to thank the LORD, for he is good. Every line ends with “for his loving kindness endures forever.” He alone does great wonders. He made the heavens, the earth, the sun, and the moon. He brought Israel out of Egypt and divided the Red Sea. He led his people through the desert and struck down kings. He remembered them when they were low. He gives food to every creature.
chapters.meaning: The same reply follows all twenty-six lines. The form fits a leader’s line and a people’s answer. The reply ties very different acts together. Creation, the exodus, and daily food are all called kindness. Verse 23 moves from old history to “us” in our low state. Verse 25 widens to food for “every creature.” The poem ends with thanks to the God of heaven.

lds.text: What does the repeated response connect across the different remembered events?

chapters.historicalNote: The repeated response connects each remembered act with enduring kindness.

contextNote.title: A repeated response binds different acts together

chapters.title: Songs withheld beside Babylon’s rivers
chapters.summary: The exiles sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept for Zion. They hung their harps on the trees. Their captors asked them for a song of Zion. They ask how they can sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land. The speaker swears never to forget Jerusalem. He asks the LORD to remember what Edom said when the city fell. He speaks of Babylon’s coming ruin. The poem ends with fierce words about repayment.
chapters.meaning: The captors request music from people who have lost their home. They want Zion’s worship as entertainment. Verse 4 links the LORD’s song with a place and with freedom. The final anger in verses 8–9 must be read beside that loss. Second Kings 25:7 shows what these people had seen. A Babylonian hymn tablet provides a comparison with another tradition of sacred songs. It does not prove that this psalm borrowed from that hymn.

lds.text: What do the withheld songs and violent ending reveal about the exiles’ grief?

chapters.historicalNote: The final wish includes killing children. It expresses revenge within the exiles’ grief and humiliation.

contextNote.title: Exile changes what a song can do

The final anger in verses 8–9 must be read beside that loss. Second Kings 25:7 shows what these people had seen. A Babylonian hymn tablet provides a comparison with another tradition of sacred songs. It does not prove that this psalm borrowed from that hymn.

chapters.title: Thanks before the mighty
chapters.summary: The speaker thanks the LORD with his whole heart. He sings praise before the “gods” and bows toward the holy temple. On the day he called, God answered and gave him strength. All the kings of the earth will thank the LORD. The LORD is high, yet he looks after the lowly. He knows the proud from far away. He keeps the speaker alive in trouble. The speaker asks him not to abandon the work of his hands.
chapters.meaning: The speaker stands among powers: “gods” in verse 1 and kings in verse 4. Verse 6 says where the highest power directs its attention. The LORD is high and looks after the lowly. He keeps the proud at a distance. He knows them “from afar.” Verse 8 holds trust and a request together. God will complete his purpose, and the speaker still asks not to be left.

lds.text: Why does the speaker end with a further request after giving thanks?

chapters.historicalNote: Confidence about rescue stands beside a final request not to abandon the work already begun.

contextNote.title: High authority notices low people
contextNote.text: The speaker stands among powers: “gods” in verse 1 and kings in verse 4. Verse 6 says where the highest power directs its attention. The LORD is high and looks after the lowly. He keeps the proud at a distance. He knows them “from afar.” Verse 8 holds trust and a request together. God will complete his purpose, and the speaker still asks not to be left.

chapters.title: Known wherever the speaker goes
chapters.summary: The LORD has searched the speaker and knows him. He knows when he sits and rises and what he will say. The speaker cannot flee from God’s Spirit. In heaven, in the grave, or across the sea, God’s hand holds him. Darkness is as light to God. God formed him in his mother’s womb. All his days were written before one of them came. He asks God to search his heart and lead him.
chapters.meaning: The poem opens with a fact: “you have searched me.” It closes in verse 23 with a request: “Search me.” Between them, being known feels close in more than one way. Verse 5 says he is hemmed in, and verse 7 speaks of fleeing. Verses 13–18 find comfort in it. After fierce words about the wicked in verses 19–22, he turns to himself. Verse 24 asks whether any wicked way is in him.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies being known by God. Why does the speaker end by asking God to examine his heart?

chapters.historicalNote: The final request invites examination of the heart after forceful words against enemies.

contextNote.title: Being known ends with an invitation to examine

chapters.title: Protection from violent people
chapters.summary: The speaker asks the LORD to rescue him from evil and violent men. They plan harm and stir up strife all day. Their tongues are sharp like a serpent’s. The proud have hidden traps and nets for him. He says the LORD is his God and covers his head in battle. He asks that their own words bring them down. He knows the LORD upholds the cause of the poor. The upright will live in God’s presence.
chapters.meaning: Verse 11 names two men together: the slanderer and the violent man. The poem has treated them as one threat throughout. Verses 2–3 describe hearts and tongues. Verses 4–5 describe hands and traps. Verse 11 says evil will “hunt” the violent man. The hunter becomes the hunted. Verse 12 states his confidence that the LORD defends the poor.

lds.text: How does the closing concern for the poor widen the speaker’s request?

chapters.historicalNote: The closing confidence turns toward justice for the poor and safety for upright people.

contextNote.title: Speech and violence belong to one threat
contextNote.text: Verse 11 names two men together: the slanderer and the violent man. The poem has treated them as one threat throughout. Verses 2–3 describe hearts and tongues. Verses 4–5 describe hands and traps. Verse 11 says evil will “hunt” the violent man. The hunter becomes the hunted. Verse 12 states his confidence that the LORD defends the poor.

chapters.title: Guard the mouth and guide correction
chapters.summary: The speaker calls on the LORD to come quickly. He asks that his prayer rise like incense. He asks God to set a guard over his mouth. He asks that his heart not lean toward evil. He does not want to share the feasts of wrongdoers. He would welcome a good person’s rebuke as a kindness. His eyes are fixed on the LORD. He asks to be kept from the traps set for him.
chapters.meaning: Most prayers for protection look outward at enemies. Verse 3 asks for protection from the speaker’s own mouth. Verse 4 adds his heart and his appetite. He fears being drawn in by what the wicked enjoy. The danger is joining them. Verse 5 welcomes correction from a righteous person. He calls such a blow kindness and oil for his head.

lds.text: Why does the speaker welcome correction while asking for protection?

chapters.historicalNote: Protection includes help against the speaker’s own harmful choices, not only outside enemies.

contextNote.title: The speaker asks protection from joining the harm
contextNote.text: Most prayers for protection look outward at enemies. Verse 3 asks for protection from the speaker’s own mouth. Verse 4 adds his heart and his appetite. He fears being drawn in by what the wicked enjoy. The danger is joining them. Verse 5 welcomes correction from a righteous person. He calls such a blow kindness and oil for his head.

chapters.title: A refuge when nobody offers help
chapters.summary: The heading sets this prayer in the cave where David hid. The speaker cries aloud and pours out his complaint. When his spirit is faint, God knows his path. Enemies have hidden a trap on the road. He looks to his right, and no one is there. No one cares about his life. He cries that the LORD is his refuge. He asks to be brought out of prison, and the righteous will gather around him.
chapters.meaning: A defender stood at a person’s right hand (see 109:31). In verse 4 that place is empty. He says refuge has fled and no one cares. Verse 5 answers the empty place: “You are my refuge.” The LORD is also his share among the living. The poem begins in isolation. Its last verse expects the righteous to gather around him.

lds.text: How would joining people who give thanks change the speaker’s loneliness?

chapters.historicalNote: The prayer names abandonment directly and asks for release into a grateful gathering.

contextNote.title: A public cry begins in isolation
contextNote.text: A defender stood at a person’s right hand (see 109:31). In verse 4 that place is empty. He says refuge has fled and no one cares. Verse 5 answers the empty place: “You are my refuge.” The LORD is also his share among the living. The poem begins in isolation. Its last verse expects the righteous to gather around him.

chapters.title: Teach me the way I should go
chapters.summary: The speaker asks the LORD to hear him and answer in faithfulness. He asks God not to bring him to judgment. No one living is righteous before God. An enemy has crushed his life and made him sit in darkness. He remembers the days of old and stretches out his hands. His soul thirsts like dry ground. He asks to hear of God’s kindness in the morning. He asks to be taught the way to go.
chapters.meaning: The speaker wants rescue from an enemy. Verse 2 makes clear he does not ask on his own merit. No living person could stand in that court. He appeals instead to God’s faithfulness (verse 1) and name (verse 11). He then asks four times to be guided or taught (verses 8 and 10). Rescue alone is not all he wants. Romans 3:20 echoes verse 2.

lds.text: How does the admission about human failure prepare for a request for guidance?

chapters.historicalNote: The request joins mercy with a desire to change direction through God’s teaching.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: A plea for rescue includes a limit on judgment
contextNote.text: The speaker wants rescue from an enemy. Verse 2 makes clear he does not ask on his own merit. No living person could stand in that court. He appeals instead to God’s faithfulness (verse 1) and name (verse 11). He then asks four times to be guided or taught (verses 8 and 10). Rescue alone is not all he wants. Romans 3:20 echoes verse 2.

chapters.title: A king asks for rescue and flourishing
chapters.summary: The speaker blesses the LORD, his rock, who trains his hands for battle. He asks what a human is, a breath and a passing shadow. He asks God to bend the heavens and come down. He asks rescue from foreigners whose mouths speak lies. He will sing a new song on the ten-stringed lyre. Then sons will grow like strong plants and daughters like carved pillars. Barns will be full and flocks many. No cry of distress will be heard in the streets.
chapters.meaning: The poem begins as a king’s prayer in wartime. Verse 12 shows what the fighting is for. The goal is ordinary life at home. Sons grow like healthy plants, and daughters stand like carved pillars. Verses 13–14 add full barns, large flocks, and quiet streets. Verse 14 names no breach, no exile, and no outcry. Peace is described in things people can see.

lds.text: What kind of life does the speaker want after the battle ends?

chapters.historicalNote: The desired outcome reaches beyond victory toward households and streets free from distress.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: A war prayer turns toward ordinary flourishing
contextNote.text: The poem begins as a king’s prayer in wartime. Verse 12 shows what the fighting is for. The goal is ordinary life at home. Sons grow like healthy plants, and daughters stand like carved pillars. Verses 13–14 add full barns, large flocks, and quiet streets. Verse 14 names no breach, no exile, and no outcry. Peace is described in things people can see.

chapters.title: Tell later generations about God’s care
chapters.summary: The speaker will praise God his King every day. One generation will tell the next of God’s mighty acts. The LORD is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger. He is good to all. His kingdom lasts through all generations. He holds up all who fall. Every creature looks to him for food at the right time. He is near to all who call on him in truth.
chapters.meaning: The word “all” or “every” runs through this poem. Verses 11–13 speak of God’s kingdom and power. Verses 14–16 show what that kingship looks like. He lifts those who fall and feeds every living thing. Verse 16 pictures an open hand. The king is known by what he provides. This is the last poem in the book that carries David’s name.

lds.text: How does care for those who fall express the king’s greatness?

chapters.historicalNote: Lasting kingship appears through care that reaches weak people and all living things.
