chapters.title: Do not put lasting hope in rulers
chapters.summary: The speaker will praise the LORD as long as he lives. He warns against trusting in princes. A human ruler dies, and his plans die that day. The one whose help is the God of Jacob is blessed. God made heaven, earth, and sea and keeps faith forever. He gives justice to the oppressed and food to the hungry. He frees prisoners and opens blind eyes. He guards foreigners, orphans, and widows.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 does not say that rulers are wicked. Verse 4 gives the reason for the warning. A ruler’s breath leaves him, and his plans end that day. Hope placed in him ends with him. Verse 6 sets God’s lasting faithfulness against that. Verses 7–9 list what a good ruler should do. The LORD does each one for the hungry, the prisoner, and the stranger.

lds.text: Why does the poem connect lasting hope with care for overlooked people?

chapters.historicalNote: Human plans end with death. The praise identifies care for the overlooked as enduring strength.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: Human mortality limits political trust
contextNote.text: Verse 3 does not say that rulers are wicked. Verse 4 gives the reason for the warning. A ruler’s breath leaves him, and his plans end that day. Hope placed in him ends with him. Verse 6 sets God’s lasting faithfulness against that. Verses 7–9 list what a good ruler should do. The LORD does each one for the hungry, the prisoner, and the stranger.

chapters.title: Praise for renewal, weather, and teaching
chapters.summary: It is good to sing praise to the LORD. He builds up Jerusalem and gathers Israel’s outcasts. He heals the brokenhearted and binds their wounds. He counts the stars and names each one. He covers the sky with clouds and feeds animals and young ravens. He takes no pleasure in a horse’s strength. He sends snow, frost, and hail, and his word melts them. He has given his word to Israel.
chapters.meaning: Verse 2 speaks of a city rebuilt and outcasts gathered. Verse 3 turns to hearts that are broken. Verse 4 turns to the number of the stars. The poem sets these side by side without comment. The one who names every star also binds wounds. Verses 10–11 say military strength does not impress him. The word that melts ice is the word given to Israel (verses 18–19).

lds.text: How does the same song connect renewal of a city with care for creatures?

chapters.historicalNote: Care for a city and care for the wider world appear within one song.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: City rebuilding and healing share one hymn
contextNote.text: Verse 2 speaks of a city rebuilt and outcasts gathered. Verse 3 turns to hearts that are broken. Verse 4 turns to the number of the stars. The poem sets these side by side without comment. The one who names every star also binds wounds. Verses 10–11 say military strength does not impress him. The word that melts ice is the word given to Israel (verses 18–19).

chapters.title: Heaven and earth join the praise
chapters.summary: The poem calls for praise from the heavens. Angels, sun, moon, and stars are told to praise the LORD. He commanded, and they were created. Then it calls for praise from the earth. Sea creatures, fire, hail, snow, and wind are named. Mountains, trees, wild animals, cattle, and birds follow. Kings and all peoples are called, young and old. The LORD’s name alone is exalted.
chapters.meaning: The list moves from the heavens down to the earth (verses 1–6, 7–12). People come last. Among people verse 11 names kings and rulers first. Verse 12 then names young men and women, old men and children. Rank gives no better place in this choir. Snow and sea creatures are called before any king. Verse 13 gives the reason: only his name is exalted.

lds.text: What changes when rulers join the same invitation as children and animals?

chapters.historicalNote: The long invitation places powerful rulers alongside creatures and people of every age.
chapters.mapNote: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

contextNote.title: A list removes rank from the invitation
contextNote.text: The list moves from the heavens down to the earth (verses 1–6, 7–12). People come last. Among people verse 11 names kings and rulers first. Verse 12 then names young men and women, old men and children. Rank gives no better place in this choir. Snow and sea creatures are called before any king. Verse 13 gives the reason: only his name is exalted.

chapters.title: A new song and a call for judgment
chapters.summary: The poem calls for a new song in the gathering of the faithful. Israel should rejoice in its Maker. The people praise with dancing, tambourine, and lyre. The LORD takes pleasure in his people and honors the humble with victory. The faithful sing for joy on their beds. Praise is in their mouths and a two-edged sword in their hands. They are to carry out the judgment that is written. This is the honor of all his faithful ones.
chapters.meaning: The poem turns sharply at verse 6. Dancing and song give way to a sword. Verse 9 limits what the sword may do. It carries out “the written judgment,” so it is not private revenge. Verse 4 says the people honored this way are the humble. The text joins worship and judgment and does not explain how. Readers have understood the time and manner in different ways.

lds.text: How does the armed ending change the meaning of the opening celebration?

chapters.historicalNote: The ending joins praise with force. Its violent images remain part of the song’s claim.
chapters.mapNote: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

contextNote.title: Celebration carries a forceful second movement
contextNote.text: The poem turns sharply at verse 6. Dancing and song give way to a sword. Verse 9 limits what the sword may do. It carries out “the written judgment,” so it is not private revenge. Verse 4 says the people honored this way are the humble. The text joins worship and judgment and does not explain how. Readers have understood the time and manner in different ways.

chapters.title: Let everything with breath praise
chapters.summary: The last psalm calls for praise to God in his sanctuary and in the heavens. He is to be praised for his mighty acts and his greatness. Praise him with trumpet, harp, and lyre. Praise him with tambourine and dancing. Praise him with strings, pipe, and loud cymbals. Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.
chapters.meaning: The poem answers four questions in order. Verse 1 says where, and verse 2 says why. Verses 3–5 say how, and verse 6 says who. Verses 3–5 name trumpet, strings, drums, dancing, flute, and cymbals. An Egyptian harp shows one ancient form of a string instrument. Praise uses breath, hands, skill, and the whole body. The book began with one blessed person and ends with everything that breathes.

lds.text: What does the final invitation add to the many individual prayers in the collection?

chapters.historicalNote: The collection ends with a wide invitation rather than one person’s prayer.

people.name: David
people.role: King named in many psalm headings
people.relations: Some headings connect songs with Saul, Absalom, and other people in David’s life.
people.meaning: The collection remembers his worship, dangers, failures, and the promise concerning his royal line.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Solomon
people.role: King named in two headings
people.relations: Psalm 72 concerns a just ruler. Psalm 127 concerns work, rest, and children.
people.meaning: These associations place royal justice and household care within the collection.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Asaph
people.role: Name attached to a group of psalms
people.relations: The headings name Asaph in Psalm 50 and Psalms 73–83.
people.meaning: The songs include judgment, questions about suffering, remembered history, and appeals after destruction.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Jeduthun
people.role: Musician named in three headings
people.relations: The headings connect his name with musical directions for the songs.
people.meaning: His name recalls the performance of prayers, not only their written words.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: The sons of Korah
people.role: Group named in worship-song headings
people.relations: Their songs include longing for God, national defeat, Zion, and unanswered distress.
people.meaning: The group’s songs preserve different experiences of worship rather than one steady mood.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Heman the Ezrahite
people.role: Name in Psalm 88’s heading
people.relations: The heading also names the sons of Korah. The prayer describes isolation and approaching death.
people.meaning: The associated prayer continues without a closing answer or promise of immediate relief.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Ethan the Ezrahite
people.role: Name in Psalm 89’s heading
people.relations: The song recalls a promise to David and asks about the king’s present humiliation.
people.meaning: The prayer holds remembered promise beside a difficult present experience.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Moses
people.role: Leader remembered in songs and a heading
people.relations: The collection recalls his work with Aaron and his prayers during the people’s failures.

people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Aaron
people.role: Priest remembered with Moses
people.relations: The songs name his descendants, his prayers, and the people’s conduct toward him.

people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Samuel

people.name: Abraham

people.name: Isaac

contextGuide.title: Psalms: context and evidence
contextGuide.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A song can move without erasing its beginning
steps.text: The first line accuses and still says “my God” twice. The speaker complains to the one he feels has left. The poem then swings between pain and memory. Complaint and memory alternate through verses 1–10. From verse 22 it becomes praise. Verse 24 says God has not hidden his face. Jesus speaks the first line on the cross in Mark 15:34.

steps.title: Some prayers end without visible relief
steps.text: This is the one prayer in the book with no turn toward hope. Its last word is “darkness.” Yet verse 1 calls the LORD “the God of my salvation.” The speaker says three times that he keeps praying (verses 1, 9, 13). His faith shows in the fact that he still speaks. The book of Psalms includes this prayer with the rest. A person may pray this way and still be praying.

steps.title: Exile changes what a song can do
steps.text: The captors request music from people who have lost their home. They want Zion’s worship as entertainment. Verse 4 links the LORD’s song with a place and with freedom. The final anger in verses 8–9 must be read beside that loss. Second Kings 25:7 shows what these people had seen. A Babylonian hymn tablet provides a comparison with another tradition of sacred songs. It does not prove that this psalm borrowed from that hymn.

steps.title: Praise includes bodies, skills, and many sounds
steps.text: The poem answers four questions in order. Verse 1 says where, and verse 2 says why. Verses 3–5 say how, and verse 6 says who. Verses 3–5 name trumpet, strings, drums, dancing, flute, and cymbals. An Egyptian harp shows one ancient form of a string instrument. Praise uses breath, hands, skill, and the whole body. The book began with one blessed person and ends with everything that breathes.
